entries.title: Bears gives update to NFL stadium committee
entries.summary: <p>The Bears presented an update on their stadium location search to the NFL’s stadium subcommittee Wednesday. Bears chairman George McCaskey and president/CEO Kevin Warren briefed the group on their progress in both Indiana and Illinois, a source confirmed.</p><p>The presentation was in coordination with the NFL’s quarterly meetings in New York City and not because of any pending agreement. The Bears have given similar updates in the past.</p><p>The Bears want to get a stadium funding deal done during the Illinois general assembly’s veto session, which ends Dec. 3. Two weeks ago, the Bears said they were finalizing due diligence details across their two sites in the Wolf Lake area of Hammond, Indiana, but also had been engaged with Illinois legislators about staying in-state. NFL commissioner Roger Goodell has met at least three times with Illinois politicians.</p><p>The Bears own 326 acres in Arlington Heights. In recent weeks, developers from sites across Chicago have pitched their land as a potential landing spots, though without any coordination with the team.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: White Sox send Luis Castillo, Davis Martin to Rockies in four-player swap, shedding payroll
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> general manager Chris Getz sure isn’t hesitant to move off a mistake.</p><p>When Seranthony Dominguez pitched his way out of the closer role early in the first season of a two-year, $20 million contract, Getz dumped his salary in a trade deadline deal that brought back former three-time All-Star starting pitcher Luis Castillo.</p><p>Now, he’s doing it again.</p><p>In a surprise move pulled hours after officially introducing right-handed starter Dustin May on Thursday, the White Sox traded Castillo and right-hander Davis Martin to the Colorado Rockies in exchange for left-handed starter Sean Sullivan and 17-year-old catching prospect Douglas Veliz.</p><p>It’s reflected in the strength of the return, but the primary appeal to the Sox is salary relief, as the Rockies are expected to pay the remaining $22.5 million owed to Castillo in 2027; the final year of the 33-year-old’s contract. The White Sox front office has been openly targeting starting pitching, in a free-agent market with several such options that could draw a price similar or greater than the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/11/19/white-sox-banking-on-dustin-mays-untapped-upside-and-still-hunting-for-more-additions" target="_blank" ><u>three-year, $52.5 million deal the club just signed with right-hander Dustin May</u></a>.</p><p>Now, the Sox have $22.5 million more room in their budget with which to chase an impact addition, and improve upon the failed attempt to find that impact in Castillo.</p><p>“I anticipate activity,” said Getz on Thursday afternoon, in a prescient answer on whether he expected to complete more acquisitions before an anticipated MLB lockout on Dec. 1. “When this press conference is finished, we are going to continue to get on the phone and get to work and find ways for us to get better. We are very specific in our targets and we know what our needs are, and we are going to try to get as much done as we can.”</p><p>The rub is how much the deal reveals the cost for the mistake of acquiring Castillo, whom — as Getz readily acknowledged in September — saw his stuff back up before succumbing to shoulder bursitis, and posting an 8.42 ERA in a White Sox uniform.</p><p>Martin was sensational in the first two months of 2026, before a rough second half saw him fall out of the postseason pitching mix. But up until Thursday night, Getz noted that Martin was hindered by a right calf issue for most of the season, and the club was optimistic about the 29-year-old’s potential to return to form when healthy; which has been that of a solid-average back-end of the rotation starter over the last two years. Moreover, Martin was the longest-tenured player on the team, a respected clubhouse voice and one of the roster’s MLBPA sub-representatives.</p><p>“During his time with us Davis has been the ultimate professional, great teammate and mentor to the pitching staff,” Getz said in a statement. “He has meant a lot to this organization and to his teammates. We thank him and wish him the very best.”</p><p>The return is not exactly negligible.</p><p>A long-levered lefty whose unique delivery helps offset his high-80s velocity, Sullivan had a ugly statline in his major-league debut this year (8.87 ERA in 22 ⅓ innings), but league scouts feel he can be useful starter depth, and certainly will be helped by escaping the challenge of pitching in Denver’s hitter-friendly atmosphere. Veliz is obviously very far away, having only played in the Dominican Summer League and his defensive future is hard to pin down. But one NL scout liked his contact ability and bat speed in his professional debut season.</p><p>It’s just that neither are serious candidates to fill out opening day slots in a starting rotation the White Sox are seeking to upgrade, while two potential ones were just sent out. Instead, the Sox are planning to throw money at that issue, and they can’t afford to make a mistake with that move.</p><p>Then again, clearly Getz would find a way to move on, even if they do.</p>

entries.title: Grand Theft Auto VI release turned into real-life workout at Roscoe Village gym
entries.summary: <p>Wolfgang Weidler had been counting down to the release of Grand Theft Auto VI for months. By Thursday morning, he'd already spent an hour playing the highly anticipated video game before heading to work at Crosstown Fitness in Roscoe Village, where he’s a trainer.</p><p>He was so engrossed, he said, that he lost track of time.</p><p>“Oh, my gosh – it is so immersive,” Weidler said. “You can literally talk to any non-playable character … you literally get sucked in.”</p><p>The latest installment in the hugely popular Grand Theft Auto franchise, GTA VI has already generated an estimated $1.84 billion in revenue as of release day, based on sales of about 19 million copies, according to market research firm Sensor Tower. The game is the first new main installment in the series in 13 years.</p><p>But Weidler, 22, didn't want to simply celebrate the game's release at home. He brought its fictional, Miami-inspired setting of Vice City to the gym, transforming three classes scheduled for 10 a.m., noon and 4:30 p.m. Thursday into a GTA VI experience.</p><p>The setup included six workout stations with exercise names like “Run From The Cops” and “Break Open The Vault,” inflatable palm trees, photoshopped graphics of gym staff members reimagined as video game characters and a playlist Weidler mixed himself, full of Latin tunes and Miami-inspired beats.</p><p>Weidler said he spent about 15 hours planning the classes, including marketing the event through a comical Instagram reel and vibrant posters.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-cf0000" It might have been November in Chicago, he told us, but the workout would feel like “July on a beach.”</p><p>Wielder also incorporated the game's star-based wanted-level system into the workout, drawing star scales on the boards listing each exercise. With every exercise, came a different storyline.</p><p>“We’re operating on the wrong side of the law this morning – we did something a little bad, and you gotta run from the cops,” he said, introducing the sprinting exercise. “When I say run, I really mean run.”</p><p>Weidler's reminders to bring the heat to Vice City kept participants moving through the intensive workout. entries.title: Family mourns 24-year-old woman killed in Rogers Park after shift caring for people with disabilities
entries.summary: <p>Family is mourning a woman killed outside her Rogers Park apartment Wednesday night after working a shift helping people with disabilities. </p><p>Bintou Salami, who recently moved to the neighborhood to be closer to her job at Misericordia Heart of Mercy, was parking a Lime scooter when someone attempted to rob her before fatally shooting her, Salami's family told the Sun-Times. </p><p>Two hours later, a 25-year-old man was found dead at the Morse CTA Red Line station. Chicago police told Salami's family they were investigating if the two deaths were connected. </p><p>"She's everything to me," said her brother, Raoufou Salami. The siblings, who moved to Chicago together two years ago, are from Togo in West Africa, where the rest of their family lives.</p><p>Salami, 24, was found with a fatal gunshot wound to her head around 11:15 p.m. in the 1400 block of West Chase Avenue and was pronounced dead at the scene, according to police. </p><p>About two hours later and a half-mile away, the 25-year-old man was found with a gunshot wound in the stairwell of the Morse station at 1358 W. Morse Ave., police said.</p><p></p><p>The CTA did not comment on the investigation Thursday.</p><p>Fiona Carey, one of Salami's neighbors, was sitting on her couch Wednesday night when she heard two gunshots outside her building.</p><p>“It’s never gunshots,” she said. “I didn’t even get up. I didn’t think it was anything.”</p><p>It wasn’t until her roommate arrived home a half hour later and saw police cars and red police tape outside that Carey realized her neighbor had been killed. entries.title: UChicago plans to build medical center offering hundreds of South Side jobs
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Plan Commission gave the first city approvals Thursday to a development in Washington Park that would be anchored by a new University of Chicago pathology lab — a project the local alderwoman praised as an economic engine for a neighborhood that was once considered for the Obama Presidential Center.</p><p>UChicago is eyeing the 8 acres at 370 E. Garfield Blvd. for a five-story lab that would create new jobs and training opportunities in the field. </p><p>The university estimates the $295 million project will create 200 jobs in phase one, which would include a six-story parking garage and pedestrian plaza.</p><p>Central to the development is what will come in phase two: a first-of-its-kind clinical lab technician training program in Chicago at a new southern campus for Malcolm X College.</p><p>Ald. Pat Dowell (3rd) said the project will be catalytic for the area around Washington Park, which is filled with vacant lots.</p><p>“I think this is big for Washington Park,” Dowell said. “Although we didn't get the Obama Center, this is better because it has more of an impact on the constituents that I represent.”</p><p>The medical center will include a food hall that’s open to the public, according to the development team. It will also bring 14,000 square feet of public green space, featuring a landscaped pedestrian plaza that offers a respite for workers and visitors of the campus.</p><p>Some <b>speakers</b> questioned why such a large parking structure was included. The site is bound by the Green Line to the west and deemed a transit-served location by the city.</p><p>UChicago’s team said with more than 1,000 workers at the site, some will need to park. They told commissioners the parking garage will also include a transit waiting area so riders can be sheltered while waiting for the bus.</p><p>Angie Marks, UChicago’s associate vice president of real estate operations, said job creation is the project's biggest goal — especially when considering additional phases. She said the medical center will be looking for other companies that would benefit from the training Malcolm X will provide when considering future partners and tenants.</p><p>David Sanders, president of Malcolm X College, said it's committed to making sure South Side residents are first in line for the new jobs. Malcolm X’s presence at the 8-acre campus comes after it expanded and renovated its Far West Side satellite campus in 2024. The campus <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/10/17/malcolm-x-college-west-campus-danny-davis-community-center" >reopened</a> in October.</p><p>“We are excited about this because it's all about upbuilding our communities,” Sanders said. “Wherever education is high, crime is low, wages are higher, and that is what we are trying to do in bringing this to the South Side. It is a tremendous opportunity, and we want to make sure that that happens.”</p><p>The Plan Commission also signed off on an apartment tower that will transform a vacant corner at the intersection of North Sheridan Road and West Diversey Parkway.</p><p>The project, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/11/06/developer-28-story-apartment-tower-lake-view" >2800 N. Sheridan Road</a>, will replace the former Ida and Norman Stone Medical Building with a 28-story apartment tower. Demolition of the medical building is currently underway.</p><p>There will be 345 apartments — 69 of them affordable — anchored by a 50,000-square-foot premier fitness club and 10,000 square feet of retail. </p><p>The affordable units will be available to those making between 40%-80% the area median income. For a two-person household, that would be an annual income of $38,880 to $77,800.</p><p>Construction would start in mid-2027 and wrap up two years later, if approved by the City Council, according to the development team. </p><p>“This is the entry to my community,” Ald. Bennett Lawson (44th) said. “This is the corner of the park, and it's an important spot.”</p>

entries.title: Eight overlooked seniors to keep an eye on during the upcoming high school basketball season
entries.summary: <p>They’ve made themselves known commodities within their own leagues but remain underrated statewide. The following showcases a nice portrait of overlooked seniors who have made their presence felt but without a whole lot of fanfare.</p><p><b>Nate Fridman, Glenbrook North</b></p><p>The 5-10 point point guard is an indispensable player for a team with big expectations this winter. He packs a punch as a fearless and entertaining player as an off-the-dribbble playmaker for himself and others. He’s started every game since his sophomore year and churned out a team-high 13.5 points and 3.6 assists a game as a junior.</p><p><b>Collin Tobin, Niles North</b></p><p>The 6-2 combo guard put together perhaps the best season no one talked about as a junior. Vastly overlooked on the recruiting trail, Tobin averaged 19 points, eight rebounds and 3.5 assists a game while being named the Central Suburban League North Player of the Year. His high usage rate should increase even more, so expect a huge encore season.</p><p><b>Jamarri Fears, Romeoville</b></p><p>Yes, it’s possible to be a Fears and be overlooked. While Jeremiah Fears is averaging 15 points a game in the NBA and Jeremy Fears is an All-American at Michigan State, younger brother Jamarri Fears is an unheralded senior. Everyone is talking about all the transfers at Romeoville, yet it’s the still-improving senior guard coming off a season where he put up 15.9 points a game who is the catalyst.</p><p><b>David Showman, Wheaton-Warrenville South</b></p><p>A perimeter player with size and space-the-floor shooting ability. With little fanfare to go with it, the 6-4 Showman put up 14.8 points a game as a junior. He connected on 66 of 171 from the three-point line while also leading the Tigers in rebounding.</p><p><b>Carson Trivellini, Crystal Lake South</b></p><p>Yes, baseball is his sport. Trivellini is headed to Illinois for baseball next year. However, the basketball career the 6-3 point guard is in the midst of putting together is off the charts. He’s already scored over 1,000 career points and has won a whopping 88 games in three years, including three regional titles and one sectional championship.</p><p><b>Logan Wessel, Mount Carmel</b></p><p>No one noticed but the 6-4 Wessel averaged 13 points and six rebounds a game with a couple of scoring outputs of 29 and 28 points. And the departure of DK Heard earlier this fall elevates the significance of having a versatile player like Wessell around.</p><p><b>Ryan Dinnon, Andrew</b></p><p>The struggles of a 13-20 season took some of the shine off the season Dinnon put together. On pace to surpass 1,000 career points this season, the 6-7 Dinnon, who is headed to Division II Wisconsin-Parkside, was terrific as a junior: 17.2 points, 8.4 rebounds and 1.7 assists a game. He’s the go-to guy for what should be a much improved and experienced Thunderbolts team.</p><p><b>Ben Whorlow, St. Francis</b></p><p>The rise of Whorlow last season led to a late-season surge for St. Francis that included a Class 3A sectional championship. He’s big and strong, pushing close to 6-9 and 230 pounds, and his postseason experience should be a boon.</p><p>Whorlow should be an even better, more confident version of after last year’s impressive numbers of 16 points, nine rebounds and three blocks a game.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-430000" name="html-embed-module-430000"></a><iframe title="No Shot Clock, Ep. 207: Revealing the 2026-27 statewide preseason Super 25 rankings" allowtransparency="true" height="150" width="100%" style="border: none; min-width: min(100%, 430px);height:150px;" scrolling="no" data-name="pb-iframe-player" src="https://www.podbean.com/player-v2/?i=u6iwm-1bb41bc-pb&from=pb6admin&share=1&download=1&rtl=0&fonts=Arial&skin=1&font-color=auto&logo_link=episode_page&btn-skin=c73a3a" loading="lazy"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p>
entries.author: Joe Henricksen

entries.title: Blackhawks start slow, lose to Blue Jackets in first game since Connor Bedard's injury
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> weren't able to dig out of an early hole in a 4-2 loss to the Blue Jackets on Thursday.</p><p>"As I told the guys between the first and second [periods], the first thing we look at between periods is where was our effort, compete and execution?" coach Jeff Blashill said. "For me, it was not good enough, not good enough, not good enough. So then don’t even talk about Xs and Os at that point. I just thought we weren’t skating."</p><p>The Hawks trailed 2-0 and had been outshot 17-7 at that point.</p><p>As the game progressed, however, they improved in all three categories and seemed to figure out some things about how to create offense <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/19/blackhawks-connor-bedard-injury-surgery-rehab-decision" >without Connor Bedard</a>. They outshot the Jackets 18-16 in the second and third periods and had an even bigger advantage in expected goals.</p><p>Cole Smith cut the deficit to 3-2 on a two-on-one rush with 16 minutes left, and the Hawks generated lots of offensive-zone time while pushing for an equalizer, but it never came. Jackets goalie Cam Talbot made his biggest save on a Roman Kantserov deflection with 94 seconds left.</p><p>"Besides a slow start, we had many opportunities where we could've had a lot of goals in that game," said Frank Nazar, who scored in a fourth consecutive game. </p><p>"Honestly, I don't think we need a reset. I think we need to keep playing the way we're playing. Just start on time [and] play like that the whole game."</p><p>The Hawks have now lost their last eight meetings against the annually mediocre Jackets, who entered Thursday having dropped five straight.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">GOAL: Cole Smith picks the corner off a rush to make it a one-goal game. <a href="https://t.co/ynOwTzYNvv">pic.twitter.com/ynOwTzYNvv</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2123614415593582811?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 20, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Kantserov’s routine</b></h3><p>On the morning of almost every game day, Kantserov can be found sprinting up and down a United Center staircase that fans will eventually use to climb to their seats that night.</p><p>It's a method to wake up his legs that he brought over from Russia, where he picked it up about four years ago.</p><p>"It's my routine," Kantserov said Thursday.</p><p>Whatever he's doing seems to be working. Kantserov has been one of the few bright spots for the Hawks so far this season. At the time he ran the stairs Thursday morning, his nine goals in 21 games had him sitting two ahead of the field in the NHL's rookie scoring race.</p><p>"After last year, I feel confidence here, but first [NHL] practice, first games was absolutely different," he said. "Now I take this [knowledge and] I feel how I can play there. It's a little bit different, but I feel confidence playing with good mates in lineup and on power play."</p><h3><b>Jackets’ coaching</b></h3><p>Jackets coach Rick Bowness, 71, made his return to the bench Thursday after missing their last three games due to a health issue.</p><p>"[It's] good to be back in the fight with these guys," Bowness told reporters.</p><p>Assistant coach Don Granato filled in during Bowness' absence. Granato is a guy who can relate to the position Jeff Blashill and the rest of the Hawks' staff find themselves in.</p><p>Granato coached the Sabres from 2021 to 2024, a period during which Sabres fans were frustrated after years of losing yet the Sabres' roster still lacked the necessary talent to accomplish much. He did relatively well in the tough situation, too, guiding them to 75-, 91- and 84-point seasons.</p><p>The Hawks, comparatively, haven't reached even the lowest of those three point marks since 2018-19. They're on pace for just 53 points this season (although thanks to the randomness of hockey, they will likely finish above that).</p>

entries.title: Judge denies pause on hemp THC product ban, prohibiting sale outside dispensaries
entries.summary: <p>Hemp-infused THC products can no longer be purchased outside of dispensaries in Illinois after a judge upheld the original timeline of the ban Thursday. </p><p>Judge Martha Pacold denied a motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, which would have delayed the onset of the ban, filed by the Illinois Healthy Alternatives Association and several businesses that sell the products.</p><p>The ban, which was set to go into effect Thursday, would halt the sale of THC-infused drinks and edibles at gas stations, convenience stores and other retailers after Gov. JB Pritzker signed a bill reclassifying products with more than 0.4 milligrams of THC as cannabis, therefore prohibiting them sold outside of dispensaries. </p><p>ILHAA President Craig Katz said the organization is considering appealing the judge's decision.</p><p>"We respectfully disagree with the judge’s decision," he said in a statement. "We look forward to further pursuing our claims in the preliminary injunction. We are exploring review in the appellate court."</p><p>Businesses who continue to sell hemp products risk fines and other enforcement by the state government.</p><p>Some Chicago businesses have warned they would have to close if the ban goes through.</p><p>"Hopefully, they extend it for a longer period of time,” South Loop Market owner Anas Masoud <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2026/11/10/illinois-hemp-thc-ban-lawsuit-businesses" >said when the ban was initially delayed</a>. “Any little bit will be great. We’re all struggling.”</p><p>The next court date is scheduled for Dec. 15.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Son hesitates to share dementia diagnosis with mom
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have a complex issue. I was recently diagnosed with dementia, and I have not told my mother yet. She is 91. She is in good health, and her mind is sharp, but over the past five years she has lost two children to cancer. I'm torn about telling her, but sooner or later, she's going to notice. I've been seeing a therapist, who tells me only I can make that decision. I don't know what to do. Please help me. — <i>UNSURE SON</i></p><p><b>DEAR SON:</b> I'm sorry to learn of this difficult chapter in your life. As you mentioned, your mother is going to notice eventually. Wouldn't it be better if you told her yourself, on your own terms, instead of waiting until some awkward incident forces you (or some other loved one) to explain it to her? As a mother, chances are, she will want to be there for her son in his time of need, no matter how old the two of you may be.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I married my husband 30 years ago. His parents have never introduced me to their friends. My husband does the same rude thing when we see old friends of his who don't know me, and it hurts my feelings. Am I being sensitive, or am I being left out on purpose? It's like if they don't acknowledge me, I'll go away. I stand there awkwardly, waiting to be introduced. Should I introduce myself? If so, what should I say? — <i>NOT IMPORTANT IN THE EAST</i></p><p><b>DEAR NOT IMPORTANT:</b> The reason for your husband's lack of manners may be that he never learned them from his parents, who appear to be ignorant of the social graces. The next time you're in this uncomfortable situation, speak up. Smile and say, "I'm their daughter-in-law (or his wife), 'Vivian.' Nice to meet you!"</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My sister's daughter is going to be a first-time mom, and I'm not happy about this. It means I'll never see my sister again. Anytime someone in my family becomes a parent, they always lie to me, assuring me things won't change, but things do change and not for the better. The new parents become impossible to talk to, and I just know this holiday season will be chaos. My wife and I have no children nor the desire to have any. Should I just avoid all family gatherings? I doubt my absence would be noticed anyway. — <i>UNHAPPY UNCLE</i></p><p><b>DEAR UNCLE:</b> Given the attitude on display in your letter, I don't think parenthood is the main reason your relatives stop talking to you. I advise you to knock that chip off your shoulder and accept that your niece didn't get pregnant to spite you. Put on your biggest smile and congratulate the new mom. When the next family gathering comes around, you may attend with a cheerful demeanor, embrace the chaos and get to know the kids; or you may stay home alone and pout. I can't make that decision for you.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Democrats need to be straight about confines of holding Trump, allies accountable
entries.summary: <p>It’s been two weeks, but many Americans are still reveling in the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/elections/photos-celebration-mourning-blue-wave-sweeps-midterms-rcna607385" target="_blank" >Democratic tsunami that swept the country Election Day</a>, brimming with excitement, teeming with hope for the future and gloating from the whooping Republicans just took.</p><p>After <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2016/11/09/500716650/donald-trump-clinches-the-presidency-in-major-upset" target="_blank" >10 long years of Donald Trump’s brute dominance over our political system</a> — whether he was in office or lurking menacingly outside of it — MAGA, the nativist, nationalist, nihilistic movement he created, was finally beaten back. And not just in the expected places — but on new frontiers like Texas, Mississippi and South Carolina.</p><p>More than <a class="Link" href="https://nolabels.org/the-latest/124-million-ballots-who-voted-in-the-2026-midterms-and-how/" target="_blank" >123 million people voted</a>, making these midterms the second-highest turnout since 1914, when neither women nor African Americans could vote.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a60000" name="module-a60000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>And ultimately, most of those millions came out for Democratic candidates, and they told us in exit polls the most important issue to them was the economy. Not surprising, but the second-most important issue was corruption and the state of democracy.</p><p>That enough Americans believed Republicans and the Trump administration’s corruption and attempts to subvert and destroy our democratic institutions were urgent enough to flip 46 House seats and nine Senate seats should be a flashing red warning for the GOP.</p><p>Now Democrats need to deliver, or at least look like they can in what will be a divided government for the next two years. That shouldn’t stop them from attempting some accountability for Trump’s large cohort of self-dealers and grifters. But they should level set with the American people about just how much they can accomplish and what “success” will actually look like.</p><p>Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/democrat-investigations-warn-trump-allies-vance-donald-jr-eric-rcna609904" target="_blank" >sent document retention letters to nearly a dozen Trump cronies and family members</a>, including his sons, Jared Kushner, Susie Wiles, Stephen Miller, Todd Blanche, Kristi Noem and more, alerting them to the fact that they will likely be called before Congress.</p><p>But before voters start salivating over potential perp walks, it’s very likely many of these folks will plead the Fifth or that they’ll refuse to testify at all. And Trump’s Department of Justice is unlikely to compel them to. Many accused of crimes will likely be offered pardons. Some may pay in some way for their actions; many will not.</p><p>As Garcia said: “Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this administration’s self-dealing, misconduct and abuse. These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans.”</p><p>Laying the groundwork for legislation that would prevent future similar corruption is incredibly important and a worthwhile pursuit. Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., put it another way recently:</p><p>“We need to make sure that a very unsexy group of people are thinking very hard about how to Trump-proof the government going forward so that no leader can do this again — no leader can enrich themselves on the backs of the American people, Democrat or Republican.”</p><p>Where Dems can be most effective, perhaps, is in exposing the rank incompetence of many Cabinet officials. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins should have to answer for the spate of foodborne illness outbreaks that happened on her watch. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. should have to answer for the measles outbreak he is responsible for. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum should have to answer for selling out our national parks. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should be impeached for war crimes.</p><p>That’s accountability, too. But if voters expect Democrats to put the Trump family and Cabinet officials behind bars, they’ll be sorely disappointed.</p><p>Dems need to be honest and forthright. Accountability will happen, but it might not look like what voters expect. Trump-proofing our government might not be the deterrent that perp walks are, but it’s the prevention that we all need.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-910000" name="module-910000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Drop in foreign student enrollment doesn’t jibe with Trump claims
entries.summary: <p>President Donald Trump has repeatedly noted the <a class="Link" href="https://perma.cc/G78U-XD4V" target="_blank" >economic boon</a> from foreign citizens who attend American universities. Yet according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.iie.org/publications/fall-2026-snapshot-on-international-student-enrollment/" target="_blank" >survey results</a> published Monday, foreign-student enrollment in the United States fell substantially this year, largely due to the uncertainty created by Trump's policies.</p><p>Based on a survey of more than 800 colleges and universities, the Institute of International Education <a class="Link" href="https://iie.widen.net/s/5dkvrgsvfv/iie_fall-2026_snapshot_full-report" target="_blank" >reported</a> that the number of new foreign students is down 15% from last year. Total international enrollment, which fell by 3% last year, decreased by 9% this year, including drops of 3% for undergraduates, 15% for graduate students, and 6% for participants in optional practical training.</p><p>That two-year decline is "likely historic," Ted Mitchell, president of the American Council on Education, <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/international-student-college-enrollment-declines.html" target="_blank" >told</a> The New York Times. And according to the survey, the most common explanations offered by institutions that saw reductions were the visa application process, U.S. travel restrictions, "feeling unwelcome in the United States" and limits on the duration of student status.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1e0000" name="module-1e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Foreign students see "too much uncertainty in the United States," NAFSA: Association of International Educators executive director Fanta Aw, whose organization represents international educators, <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/international-students-decrease-american-universities-a34e862e97509e25b93d9f2234234416" target="_blank" >told</a> the Associated Press. It is not hard to see why.</p><p>Last year, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement suddenly <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/05/23/trumps-mass-cancellation-of-student-visas-illustrates-the-lawlessness-of-his-immigration-crackdown/" target="_blank" >terminated</a> thousands of records in the database of foreign students with visas authorizing them to attend American universities. That move, which <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2025/04/25/trump-admin-reverses-termination-foreign-student-visa-registrations-00309407" target="_blank" >sowed panic</a> among students across the country, was the result of the Trump administration's "Student Criminal Alien Initiative."</p><p>Contrary to the implication of that label, the initiative affected many people who had no criminal convictions that would justify revoking their visas. Nor did ICE cite any other specific justification listed in the relevant <a class="Link" href="https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-8/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-214/subpart-A/section-214.1" target="_blank" >regulations</a>. Instead, the students were told their records had been terminated for "otherwise failing to maintain status."</p><p>Although ICE subsequently <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/04/25/trump-administration-restores-thousands-of-terminated-foreign-student-visa-records/" target="_blank" >restored</a> the records, they still included notations of the prior terminations. Those black marks, along with the possibility that ICE might reverse course again at any time, left students uncertain about whether they would be allowed to remain in the U.S. and complete their degrees — a situation that prompted <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/22/us/politics/trump-international-student-visas.html" target="_blank" >intervention</a> by a federal judge.</p><p>In July, the Department of Homeland Security <a class="Link" href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/17/2026-14439/establishing-a-fixed-time-period-of-admission-and-an-extension-of-stay-procedure-for-nonimmigrant" target="_blank" >finalized</a> a rule imposing a new four-year limit on visas for students who previously had been allowed to remain in the country until they completed their educational programs, including "authorized practical training following completion of studies." Under the new policy, students who hit the four-year limit, which is inadequate for many courses of study, would have to seek extensions from the DHS, which would have complete, unreviewable discretion to reject such requests.</p><p>In September, a federal judge <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/09/16/the-justification-for-new-time-limits-on-student-visas-borders-on-the-absurd-a-federal-judge-says/" target="_blank" >deemed</a> the rule change "arbitrary and capricious" under the Administrative Procedure Act because the DHS did not offer a plausible justification, consider alternatives, estimate predictable costs, or meaningfully respond to the points raised by commenters. U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, a George W. Bush appointee, <a class="Link" href="https://www.presidentsalliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/2026-11-16-District-Judge-dckt-73_0.pdf" target="_blank" >finalized</a> that judgment Monday, vacating the rule.</p><p>Since the Trump administration can ask a federal appeals court to review Saylor's decision, the ultimate fate of the time limit is unclear. The same goes for the $70,000 optional practical training application fee that the DHS <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/07/opt-dhs-fee-international-students-enrollment-schools/d3e3e23a-c261-11f1-8170-681419af1cc9_story.html" target="_blank" >proposed</a> last month.</p><p>All of this is hard to reconcile with what Trump has said about the benefits of hosting international students.</p><p>"I want to have foreign students," he <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2025/06/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-restricts-foreign-student-visas-at-harvard-university/" target="_blank" >insisted</a> last year. The full tuition they pay is financially essential to "our school system," he <a class="Link" href="https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-interview-laura-ingraham-fox-news-november-10-2025/" target="_blank" >explained</a>.</p><p>During his 2024 campaign, Trump <a class="Link" href="https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-interview-all-in-podcast-sacks-friedberg-june-20-2024/" target="_blank" >agreed</a> that "we need to recruit the best and brightest from the world." In fact, he <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2024/06/28/politicians-need-to-get-serious-about-retaining-foreign-graduates/" target="_blank" >said</a>, you should "automatically" get a green card when "you graduate from a college." He lamented that people who earned U.S. degrees and "desperately wanted to stay here" ended up returning to their home countries, where they started companies that employ "thousands and thousands of people."</p><p>Trump says he welcomes foreign students. His policies tell a different story.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-270000" name="module-270000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Who gets booted in Chicago? Drivers on the South Side, West Side are especially hit hard
entries.summary: <p>The last time Davorian Ware drove his 2010 Mitsubishi sedan, he was heading to Midway Airport from Champaign. It was August 2021, and he was taking a trip to Las Vegas. Before leaving, he parked in one of the city of Chicago’s overnight airport parking lots.</p><p>It was late when he got back three days later. The only thing on his mind was that he'd need to safely make the drive back to Champaign.</p><p>But Ware says, “When I came back, my car was booted."</p><p>The city’s booting program — immobilization, as city officials call it — was established in 1987. The threat that drivers with delinquent traffic tickets might find one of the yellow metal devices latched onto one of their vehicle's wheels to make it undriveable was meant as a way to get them to pay up.</p><p>But the city’s ticketing and booting hits some especially hard, a WBEZ and Chicago Sun-Times analysis of the more than 283,000 vehicles that, like Ware's, were booted by the city in the six-year span from Jan. 1, 2020, to Dec. 31, 2025, that found:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-30c88202-e466-11f1-bb83-eb39726e11be"><li>Drivers in some parts of the South Side and the West Side got booted at rates twice the citywide rate. They include Englewood, Oakland and West Garfield Park and portions of Austin, East Garfield Park, Humboldt Park and Woodlawn.</li><li>Those same areas are among communities where the highest number of drivers are on the city’s boot list. Currently, more than 1.1 million drivers are boot-eligible.</li><li>Every year, tickets from red-light and speed cameras were the leading violations for drivers whose vehicles got booted. </li><li>About 1 in 4 drivers who got booted were booted more than once.</li><li>The median amount owed by booted drivers was about $650. The most owed? More than $106,000.</li><li>About 43,000 vehicles were booted and towed during the six-year period. As of Jan. 9, more than 12,000 vehicles had not yet been returned to drivers.</li></ul><p>Critics of the program say the combination of automated enforcement, hefty ticket prices and mounting fees for delinquent traffic and parking tickets can easily exceed the ability of some drivers to be able to pay their debt. That lands them on the city’s boot list. And then the added fees they'll face for the towing and impounding of their vehicles can overwhelm them financially, ensnaring them in a debt trap for months, in some cases years.</p><p>“These debts can spiral out of control really quickly and become quite invasive in a person’s life,” says Kasey Henricks, an assistant professor in the University of Illinois Chicago's Department of Criminology, Law and Justice. "Literally taking people’s cars away is taking away their mobility in a place where their livelihood is dependent upon that.</p><p>“It completely devastates people’s lives if you have outstanding ticket debt in Chicago."</p><p>For Ware, it was the second time he'd been booted. In the course of a year and a half, he amassed 21 tickets and owed $2,811.57. He’d been on payment plans three times and defaulted each time. He says the last time was because he lost his job during the COVID-19 pandemic. Ware, says that before he got his first boot, he didn’t realized he’d racked up so many tickets nor that he was violating driving compliance laws by not having a front license plate on his car.</p><p>“I didn’t know at all, and also there was nothing I could mount" the license plate on, he says. "There weren’t any holes on the front of my bumper."</p><p>The city has a strict policy: If you default three times on payment plans, you can’t reinstate a new one unless you’re booted again, pay a reinstatement fee and pay up to 22% of the delinquent balance, depending on the plan you have. City officials say this is to discourage drivers who “constantly” default.</p><p>“They told me I gotta pay it in full,” Ware says, and that was something he couldn’t afford. His only option was to leave his car.</p><p>He didn’t know that, over the next three months, the city would tow his car to a pound. Weeks later, the city sold it at an auction for $262.08, records show. Because Ware’s car was unclaimed after 45 days, the city had that right.</p><p>Asked for comment about the WBEZ and Sun-Times findings, Mayor Brandon Johnson's office says: “The Johnson administration recognizes and understands the burden mounting debt and late penalties places on working families. To that end, building on the success of the Johnson administration’s 2025 debt amnesty effort, Mayor Johnson’s budget establishes a Vehicle Debt Amnesty Program that gives residents with outstanding tickets a path to resolve their debt by paying only the original fine while waiving all late penalties, collection costs and additional fees.”</p><p>In April 2025, the city <u>l</u>aunched two debt-relief programs — the Vehicle Violation Debt Relief Program and the Commercial Driveway and Signs Violation Debt Relief Program. Those programs allowed businesses and drivers to settle their ticket debt from tickets issued before 2024. They had two months to pay what they owed in full minus the penalties and collection fees that usually are applied. But that program concluded in June 2025.</p><p>But, also in 2025, the Johnson administration added 50 new speed cameras throughout the city. The result was a surge of speed-camera tickets. In June 2025 alone — when 22 of the new cameras came online — the city issued 240,000 speed-camera tickets, the highest amount for a single month in nearly three years, the Sun-Times and <br>WBEZ previously <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/09/02/speed-camera-ticket" target="_blank" ><u>have reported</u></a>.</p><p>Now, the City Council Office of Financial Analysis has circulated a 2027 revenue proposal that includes options to raise the city’s towing and storage fees.</p><p>In his May 2023 inaugural address, Johnson said that, even though City Hall faces big financial pressures, closing the budget gap needed to be addressed “without breaking the backs of working people.”</p><p>But the weight of the compounding costs that drivers face when they fall behind on parking and traffic tickets is heaviest in Black, working-class communities.</p><p>“Most of the consequences for late penalties, collection fees, being placed on the boot, tow and impoundment lists are concentrated for cars … in majority Black neighborhoods and, to a lesser extent but still prominent in majority-Latinx communities, too,” Henricks says.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-a10000" name="html-embed-module-a10000"></a><div style="min-height:815px" id="datawrapper-vis-VwQzB"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/VwQzB/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-VwQzB"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/VwQzB/full.png" alt="Whose vehicles get booted (Choropleth map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>‘Double punishment’</b></h3><p>Ware eventually found another job and figured his booting nightmare was in the past. But then, in February 2023, nearly a year and a half after he’d last seen his Mitsubishi, he noticed his paycheck was short by about $310.</p><p>“It was a terrible time when they started garnishing my wages,” Ware says.</p><p>City Hall had gone through the Illinois state comptroller’s Local Debt Recovery Program to collect from Ware. This program lets municipalities go after outstanding debts that otherwise would be tough to collect.</p><p>“That’s double punishment," Ware says. "If y’all took my car, at least wipe away the slate, or give me my car back."</p><p>His checks were garnished for four months.</p><p>“I ended up having a kid right before they started garnishing my wages, and we [were] trying to do daycare,” he says.</p><p>Asked what his reaction would be were he in Ware’s situation, city Comptroller Michael Belsky says, “I wouldn’t be happy about it.”</p><p>Belsky says the city tries to avoid situations like Ware found himself in.</p><p>“We don’t want people to be making a choice between paying their tickets and childcare and healthcare and food,” he says. But "if you do violate the law, we expect you to pay, but pay something.”</p><p>Belsky says 75% of drivers who get a ticket pay up.</p><p>“Where people run into problems is when they don’t pay," he says. "They just get these escalating fines on top of it, and that’s when it becomes a burden.”</p><p>Drivers who get a ticket in Chicago are mailed a notice of the violation. They have 21 days to pay. If they don’t or if they fight the ticket within 25 days after that initial 21 days, they’ll get a notice of final determination. At that point, the original fine doubles or otherwise increases up to $250.</p><p>Once drivers have at least three tickets in final determination status — or two tickets, if they’re at least a year old — the city issues a seizure notice and places their vehicle on the boot list.</p><p>Then, once a vehicle gets booted, drivers have 24 hours to pay their debt or make a deposit on a payment plan. They can request an additional 24 hours. They also are responsible for a $100 fee to remove the boot. If drivers don’t respond within that time, the city will tow and impound the car, adding a $150 tow fee for sedans to sport-utility vehicles and $250 for pickup trucks, plus a $50 daily storage fee for the time the vehicle is held at one of the city’s auto pounds.</p><p>If a vehicle hasn’t been claimed after 45 days, the driver might not be able to get it back. The city then has the right to claim the vehicle, auction it off or dispose of it.</p><h3>How the booters find you</h3><p>The city uses “license-plate technology to read plates that match against their seizure list,” according to a Department of Finance spokesperson.</p><p>Cameras are attached to the booter trucks and, using artificial intelligence, the city trucks scan the plates of every car on a block to check it against the department’s seizure list. The booter is responsible for verifying that the machine accurately identified the plate as a match on the list. Once confirmed, the city workers places a boot on the vehicle.</p><p>Belsky points to the city’s Clear Path Relief program, which allows drivers with incomes at or below 300% of the federal poverty level to pay off the original violation amount for tickets within three years, and then any other debt will be forgiven. That doesn't include parking-meter debt.</p><p>“If they pay their current tickets going back three years, we waive everything in the past as long as they stay on a payment plan for a year," Belsky says. "That also applies to booted vehicles."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-400000" name="html-embed-module-400000"></a><div style="min-height:815px" id="datawrapper-vis-kkTHY"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/kkTHY/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-kkTHY"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/kkTHY/full.png" alt="Motorists on the boot list (Choropleth map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>‘Barbaric and unjust’</b></h3><p>Lower-income drivers on the South Side and the West Side have the hardest time keeping up with the tickets, fines and fees, WBEZ and the Sun-Times found, with six ZIP codes topping the list in terms of booted vehicles per 1,000 vehicles in those areas. Median household incomes in those ZIP codes range from $34,000 to $54,000 a year. Their boot rates were twice as high as the rate citywide in those areas, which include Englewood, Oakland and West Garfield Park and portions of Austin, East Garfield Park, Humboldt Park and Woodlawn.</p><p>Chicago’s ticketing program is “probably one of the most regressive ticketing programs in the country,” according to Mark Wallace, executive director of the group Citizens to Abolish Red Light Cameras, which sued he city for failing to comply with its own rules about how red-light camera tickets are handled. In 2017, the city agreed to settle for $38.75 million, providing relief to drivers who received red-light camera tickets.</p><p>According to the WBEZ and Sun-Times analysis, red-light and speed camera tickets are the leading violations that land drivers on the boot list.</p><p>“I just think that the city is not very creative in trying to find ways to expand the tax base but find the easiest way to collect revenue, and those easiest ways tend to prey on lower-income Black and brown communities,” Wallace says.</p><p>Belsky says City Hall doesn't target those communities and that the “technology is not biased.”</p><p>He says the city is fair in how it looks for boot-eligible cars.</p><p>“We have 74 booting zones, and there’s a kind of a schedule of implementation of enforcement, but it’s also data driven,” Belsky says. “If there are areas that we get a lot of complaints from aldermen or 311 or 911 [calls], we will focus resources there. But we also try to be very equitable by having these zones.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" on,” with things like street cleaning and making sure that cars aren't in bus and bike lanes. </p><p>“There [aren’t] revenue goals,” Belsky says. “Our focus is to prevent accidents, promote public safety. We had [an] individual who worked for the city that was hit in a bike lane recently and killed. So that’s one too many.”</p><p>In June, Riley O’Neil, a city employee who worked on strategies to make streets safer for cyclists and pedestrians, was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/06/07/cyclist-death-bridgeport-crash-chicagos-safe-streets-program" target="_blank" ><u>killed</u></a> while riding his bike in a bike lane. O’Neil hit the door of a driver exiting a vehicle, which threw him into traffic and under the rear wheels of a semi-truck. The driver of the car received a citation for illegally parking his car.</p><p>Wallace calls the city’s booting program “barbaric and unjust” and says it should be a “last resort” to improve traffic safety. He says city officials need to reform the system and do a better job of notifying drivers when they’re on the boot list. He says the rules aren't clear enough and that many drivers end up being surprised when they walk “outside of their house or walking outside of their job and getting a boot on [their] car because they didn’t pay two tickets.”</p><p>Penney McDonald says she's among those who've been surprised. She grew up and learned to drive in Chicago Heights, where she says parking violations aren’t as routinely enforced.</p><p>So when McDonald moved to the South Side in 2013, she wasn’t expecting to get hit with so many tickets — mostly for parking in tow zones — that got her booted at least three times. “I never seen a ticket in my life, and I was driving a long time before I came to the city, and I never experienced that.”</p><p>Years later, she moved to Uptown and went to beauty school nearby in Rogers Park, densely populated neighborhoods where parking is hard to come by. McDonald admits that she gambled with parking in prohibited areas, hoping that a space would become available where she could park legally .</p><p>“But by the time you get to your car, you already got a ticket,” she says.</p><p>From May 2014 to June 2026, between McDonald and another driver who had access to her car, she had gotten 44 tickets, with fines totaling nearly $6,000, records show.</p><p>That’s roughly one ticket every three months. McDonald couldn't keep up. With fines from a steady flow of tickets, plus penalties for late payments, she was constantly on the boot list.</p><p>“Call me a conspiracy theorist or whatever, but it just seems like, once you’re in their system, you’re not getting out of it, and it’s overbearing,” McDonald says.</p><p>According to city records, McDonald established at least 15 payment plans, but she says she was in a tough spot financially and defaulted on more than 11 of them. Unless you got a good PTA, that comes out of the pocket of the parents.”</p><p>One time when her car was impounded after it was booted and towed, McDonald was pregnant with her middle daughter. entries.title: After 34 years bartending at Hopleaf in Andersonville, Mighty Slim has poured his last beer
entries.summary: <p>Mighty Slim is mighty thankful.</p><p>The beloved bartender with a memorable moniker poured his last beer Friday after 34 years of working behind the pine at Hopleaf, a destination craft beer tavern in Andersonville.</p><p>Ask his real name and he'll sidestep and tell you he just goes by Mighty Slim and has so for decades. Most just say Slim. His wife calls him Mighty.</p><p>About 60 well-wishers attended a sendoff Saturday. </p><p>"I'm just really surprised and kind of gobsmacked that people are interested in this. I kind of just figure I'm a bartender, and I just do my job as best I can. It's been really heartwarming," said Slim, 63.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-100000" decade ago.</p><p>"It's a young person's game, and Hopleaf is a very high volume bar and you sometimes have to step aside and let the kids do it," Slim said of his decision to retire. "I wanted to go out at the top of my game, and I think I've done that."</p><p>Hopleaf owner Mike Roper, who opened his doors a year before hiring Slim, was happy for his old friend but sad to see him go.</p><p>"He was that friendly first impression for new people, and for regulars he was a comforting familiarity," Roper said. "He was also an amazingly fastidious person. You should see his garage."</p><p>Slim wishes he had jotted down the tales he heard at the bar. If he had, he might be working on the outline of a book this week instead of cleaning out the kitchen junk drawer of his Edgewater home.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div his phone for reminders like "Frank the Pipefitter."</p><p>Last year, one of those regulars left a $1,000 tip. "Is that right?" Slim asked the guy. "Yeah. I want you to have it," he said.</p><p>He spent more than half his life at the bar.</p><p>For a long time, Slim had a rock-a-billy look. When he lost the hair he needed to slick back to complete it, he compensated by growing a long goatee, he said with a laugh.</p><p>Slim grew up in Dunning, attended Steinmetz High School, went to Wilbur Wright College and worked as a graphic artist before bartending became his profession.</p><p>He was dubbed Mighty Slim by his older brother who was in a punk band and had adopted the stage name Buddha Slim.</p><p>"I had just turned 21 and he was like, 'You have to have a 'Slim' name,'" said Slim.</p><p>About 15 years ago, to avoid long-winded explanations, he dropped the 'Mighty' when introducing himself.</p><p>It will remain mothballed in retirement, said Slim who plans to, basically, take it easy for a while.</p><p>"I think I'm going to brew some beer, read some books, do some gardening — all the stuff you don't have time to do when you're working, doing laundry, getting groceries."</p><p>Oh, and exploring Indiana, he wants to do more of that.</p><p>"Everyone from Chicago always goes up to Wisconsin, but Indiana is right there," said Slim.</p>

entries.title: Review: ‘Engines and Instruments of Flight’ at Jackalope Theatre
entries.summary: <p>In “Engines and Instruments of Flight,” Calamity West’s grandly scoped, highly unusual, decidedly niche play about playwriting, there’s a passage — from a kind-of-Greek chorus of playwright-narrators — regarding whether writers should be concerned with how popular a play will be. The conclusion is that, given the figurative blood and literal tears that go into creating anything of artistic ambition, of course a playwright cares a whole lot about their work becoming popular. West has been working on this one for a decade, and it’s one of the wonderfully weird contradictions here that she has managed to create something wildly ambitious and impressive that she knows full well will be destined to be seen by a subset of a subset of a limited market.</p><p>Not only is this a play about writing a play (and even theater lovers like me get skeptical about that notion), it’s an imaginative take on the creation of a specific play: “Angels in America.” “Engines,” receiving its world premiere at West’s home base Jackalope Theatre in Edgewater, in a brisk and buoyant production directed by Jonathan Berry, might be enjoyable to the brave someone who doesn’t know Tony Kushner’s two-part masterpiece from the 1990s, but it is so intentionally derivative of its source that its relentless cleverness will only be fully appreciated by those who do.</p><p>It’s manna for the fairly few. And there’s something extremely admirable about that.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="3.5" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> ‘Engines and Instruments of Flight’ </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-280000" name="module-280000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When:</b> Through Dec. 19<br><b>Where:</b> Jackalope Theatre in the Broadway Armory Park (5917 N. Broadway.)<br><b>Tickets:</b> $20-$45<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="http://jackalopetheatre.org" target="_blank" ><u>jackalopetheatre.org</u></a><br><b>Run time:</b> 2 hours and 45 minutes with two intermissions</div> </div><p>“Engines” tells the story (well, not “the” story, but clearly a made-up story) of how Kushner (or rather, what West would consider “a manifestation of a fictional representation” of Kushner) came to write the Pulitzer- and Tony-winning “Angels.” It’s fair to consider it an homage, even though “Engines” not only has West’s voice, but she also eventually appears as a character.</p><p>At the start, the talented six-member cast gives us a quick bio of Kushner, and then a quick sort-of bio of West, including the first time she read “Angels in America” (she didn’t “get” it), and leading up to a time she was sitting in City Lights Bookstore in San Francisco, rereading the play and becoming obsessed with it.</p><p>They also explain upfront that “Engines” is not really “about” Kushner or “Angels.” They’re not quite sure what it is about, but something bigger, maybe the idea that something has to happen in someone’s head before big changes can happen in life, or in the world. They’ll return many times to tell us other things the play is or isn’t about, none of which should be considered trustworthy. This is a play in constant state of figuring itself out, which explains why Tianxuan Chen's set design so clearly suggests a construction zone.</p><p>We then launch into the very New York life of this “Tony” (Niko Kourtis, who bears a strong resemblance to Kushner) at a time when AIDS was spreading fast and served as a death sentence. He doesn’t leave the house much, nor write much, and his miserable malaise causes his longtime boyfriend, Henry (Raphael Diaz) to leave him. The only company he keeps is his playwrights’ group, although Tony himself always arrives empty-handed.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Julian Hester (from left), Mary Williamson, Andrew Burden Swanson, Niko Kourtis and Johnard Washington portray members of a playwriting group in “Engines and Instruments of Flight: A Fantasia in Three Acts by Calamity West.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Joel Maisonet</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The members of this group form a core set of original, quite complex characters who also sometimes bear resemblances to characters in “Angels” — Gene, a caustically pragmatic African American nurse (Johnard Washington); William, a horny, guilt-filled closeted white man (Julian Hester); his suspicious girlfriend, Eleanor (Mary Williamson); and Calvin, her better-suited, always-kind suitor (Andrew Burden Swanson). In this case, though, they are all playwrights, and therefore often talk about — you guessed it — playwriting, and in critiquing each other’s work (or lack of it), they are often more competitive and cruel than supportive.</p><p>This part of “Engines” is a play I haven’t seen before and feels fully West<b>, </b>whose new play "FEAST!" will premiere at the Goodman Theatre in February.<b> </b>Other elements, such as the ghostly appearances of Ethel Rosenberg (Diaz, even better here) and Roy Cohn (Williamson, stealing the show), bear such close resemblance to “Angels” that it feels like West wrote this in part because she just <i>had</i> to try these characters on, and she clearly had a blast doing so.</p><p>West borrows “Angels’” subtitle, referring to the play as a “fantasia,” which she takes to mean she can do whatever she wants at any time. It’s arguably what she admires so much about Kushner’s play, and it’s important to appreciate when she is choosing to do exactly what Kushner did (for example, characters appear in each other’s dreams) and when she’s putting her twist on that (her angel is extremely different than the original).</p><p> For a play that’s inspired so completely by a previous one, this is a surprisingly inspired and even epic work. It’s certainly not a parody, which would be far more typical. West is more interested in challenging herself to be equally thoughtful, and she does genuinely capture the feeling of fear about AIDS at the time. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: He's leaving leadership, but House Speaker Welch's campaign funds likely still hold millions of dollars
entries.summary: <p>Even with Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch, D-Hillside, announcing under pressure he won’t run again for the influential speaker post, he still could maintain political power — whether or not he decides to ultimately resign his General Assembly seat or gets booted in an upcoming election.</p><p>Money is the most obvious reason — with the People for Emanuel Chris Welch campaign fund reporting $9.6 million on hand at the end of September, according to Illinois State Board of Elections records showing Welch as chairman of the fund and political aide TaQuoya McConnico as treasurer.</p><p>A campaign account called Democrats for the Illinois House, which Welch and McConnico also helm, reported about $4.8 million on hand.</p><p>The Team Welch for 7th District State Central Committeeperson campaign account, which he and McConnico also oversee, had about $325,000 on hand last quarter.</p><p>The Democratic Party of Proviso campaign fund, also run by Welch and McConnico, had more than $30,000 on hand on Sept. 30, records show.</p><p>In all, that’s nearly $15 million — one of the largest batches of campaign cash in Illinois. However, that was the tally before the Nov. 3 election, for which the Democrats spent big, and a current balance won't be known until after the end of the year when quarterly disclosure reports are due to the elections board.</p><p>Either way, given Illinois’ notoriously lax regulations, Welch maintains wide discretion on how to spend his campaign money moving forward, including on campaign efforts benefiting his remaining political allies, and future candidates for elected office.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure future.</p><p>Though campaign cash is supposed to be used only for political or governmental purposes, there’s also discretion over what that entails, so seeing expensive meals and entertainment expenses on Welch’s campaign accounts isn’t unusual.</p><p>People for Emanuel Chris Welch reported spending more than $275,000 with a South Side limousine service since 2022, with more than 500 payments between $60 and $3,150, records show. Election disclosure records mention only that the purpose of those expenditures was for “travel.”</p><p>The campaign fund spent more than $100,000 over the last few years on what is described in disclosure records as “meals,” including $1,000 this year on five meals at the swanky Chicago Cut Steakhouse downtown.</p><p>Neither Welch nor McConnico would respond to requests for comment.</p><p>Welch also maintains committeeman positions, including in Proviso Township, meaning that he stands to maintain a voice in the Democratic Party in the west suburbs, and throughout Illinois, should he hold onto those posts.</p><p>Welch also helped launch a nonprofit in 2024 called Black Excellence in Bleu, which in its first year raised over $1 million, some of that from groups with a stake in his legislative decision making. for Chicago-based Ancel Glink, P.C., since 2018 or 2019, serving as “of counsel” since his 2021 ascent to the speaker’s job — which he was elected to despite allegations that he had once slammed an ex-girlfriend's head on a countertop, among other disturbing accusations. Welch has denied any violence and was not charged with a crime.</p><p>His alleged mishandling of more-recent sexual harassment accusations against a political ally helped spur a House backlash that led to his decision not to try to keep the speaker post. It appears he plans to hold onto his legislative seat as a rank-and-file lawmaker, but some wonder whether he eventually will, and should, abandon that.</p><p>Ancel Glink plays a role in local campaigns, with the company and its lawyers, besides Welch, giving more than $150,000 to local political organizations and figures since 2019, according to elections board records.</p><p>The firm has also been paid more than $300,000 since then by local campaign funds, including those benefiting Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle, who doubles as the head of the Cook County Democratic Party.</p><p>A Welch campaign contributor who asked not to be named said Welch's continued level of power obviously "depends on how he's going to move forward."</p><p>But the donor added: "Do I think he has the ability to still be a player? entries.title: Christkindlmarket to celebrate 30 years of shopping, Glühwein and tradition at Daley Plaza
entries.summary: <p>Leigh Ellen Buehler has a standing date on the first Wednesday of every December with a group of girlfriends, a few German beers and one beloved Chicago holiday tradition.</p><p>“We love the hourlong train ride in, and we bring a bottle of Champagne and we all cheers and toast,” says the Downers Grove resident who has made Chicago’s Christkindlmarket an annual day out with her girlfriends for more than a decade. “And then on the way home, we Uber.”</p><p>That’s because there are “too many bags,” she said with a laugh.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1b0000" name="module-1b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Christkindlmarket 2026 </h3><br><b>Where:</b> Daley Plaza, 50 W. Washington St.; Gallagher Way, 3635 N Clark St., and RiverEdge Park, 360 N. Broadway, Aurora<br><b>When:</b> Nov. 20–Dec. 24 (Wrigleyville location is open through Dec. 31)<br><b>Tickets:</b> Free admission<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://www.christkindlmarket.com/" target="_blank" >christkindlmarket.com</a></div> </div><p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7d0000" name="image-7d0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a8a9398/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2F81%2F88945c434536b59a97bdc3d46473%2Fchristkindlmarket-112324-09.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0b40bc9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2F81%2F88945c434536b59a97bdc3d46473%2Fchristkindlmarket-112324-09.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6d2bf31/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2F81%2F88945c434536b59a97bdc3d46473%2Fchristkindlmarket-112324-09.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A display of Christmas-inspired gifts at the Christkindlmarket at Daley Plaza, Friday, Nov. 22, 2024. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6d2bf31/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2F81%2F88945c434536b59a97bdc3d46473%2Fchristkindlmarket-112324-09.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/83691f6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2F81%2F88945c434536b59a97bdc3d46473%2Fchristkindlmarket-112324-09.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6d2bf31/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2F81%2F88945c434536b59a97bdc3d46473%2Fchristkindlmarket-112324-09.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Visitors enjoy a display of Christmas-inspired gifts at the Christkindlmarket in 2024.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Buehler is one of the countless Chicagoans who have made Christkindlmarket at Daley Plaza, 50 W. Washington St., an annual holiday tradition. Christkindlmarket opens for the season on Nov. 20; the markets in Wrigleyville and Aurora also open on the same day.</p><p>“I just love when I go and step into the market in downtown Chicago,” said Maren Biester Priebe, CEO and general manager of German American Events, which organizes Christkindlmarket.</p><p>“One of my favorite feelings is that I am in this small alpine village kind of atmosphere with the red and white striped vendor huts and the Glühwein in my hands — and then I look up and I just see this amazing, beautiful, architecturally gorgeous cityscape,” Priebe said. “I don't know where else you can get that.”</p><p>This year, the German-inspired holiday market celebrates its 30th anniversary at Daley Plaza.</p><p>“Thirty years — that's a very proud number for a cultural event in the city of Chicago to be celebrating,” said Priebe, who recently marked her 20th year with the organization. “People make decisions nowadays based on what they can afford — and admission is still free to this event. We are very proud of that.”</p><p>To mark the milestone, this year’s mug features fireworks bursting over the Chicago skyline and shoppers bustling around the Christkindlmarket. Available empty or with hot beverages, the mug’s pearl-white finish has already become quite a topic of discussion among organizers.</p><p>“We internally call this color Chamonix,” said Priebe with a laugh, referring to the warm and creamy off-white color inspired by the snowy peaks of the French Alps. “It's super fancy, because it's a fancy year this year.
