entries.title: The Army plans to detonate a toxic lead compound near the Illinois- Iowa border. Here’s what to know.
entries.summary: <p>The U.S. Army is scheduled to detonate a stockpile of lead azide, a chemical used for making bombs, Monday in Middletown, Iowa, about 80 miles southwest of the Quad Cities.</p><p>The explosion is expected to create a dust plume containing lead that may cross into <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois" target="_blank" ><u>Illinois</u></a>. Lead is toxic to humans and animals. Late Thursday, the Army moved the planned explosion from Friday to Monday after politicians from Iowa and Illinois asked for a delay. The environmental organization Earthjustice also sued to try to pause the detonation. </p><p>“Public safety is the Army’s top priority,” acting secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in part of a statement posted on X. “This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-990000" name="html-embed-module-990000"></a><div style="min-height:355px" id="datawrapper-vis-oMfQV"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/oMfQV/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-oMfQV"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/oMfQV/full.png" alt="Locator map" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Here’s what else you need to know.</p><h3><b>Why is the army detonating old munitions?</b></h3><p>There’s a risk that these stored materials will detonate on their own and moving them could also trigger an explosion, according to the Defense Department. The issue was discovered earlier this year and plans to blow them up have been ongoing for months.</p><h3><b>When is this detonation going to happen?</b></h3><p>The detonation is expected to take place at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, Monday. The plant is around 80 miles southwest of the Quad Cities and only about 10 miles west of rural Illinois communities just across the Mississippi River.</p><h3><b>Has the Army blown up lead azide before? </b></h3><p>While the Army has destroyed weapons and materials in the past, it has never blown up such a large amount of this particular chemical, according to a spokesperson.</p><p>“We detonate all the time, but we have not detonated lead azide at this quantity,” said Lori McFate, public affairs specialist with the Army Sustainment Command in Bettendorf, Iowa.</p><p>McFate said the explosion will take place after months of planning. The procedure has received a green light from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency regional office in Kansas City. That’s a different jurisdiction than the regional EPA office in Chicago, which oversees environmental protection in Illinois.</p><h3><b>What is lead azide?</b></h3><p>Lead azide is a compound of lead and nitrogen, used to make bombs. About 5 tons of it will be blown up Monday.</p><p>“The lead azide has aged. It's become unstable to the point where moving it or even allowing it to sit on the odd chance that it receives some sort of shock or friction could lead to a spontaneous explosion,” said Greg Domski, associate provost and professor of chemistry and biochemistry at Augustana College in Rock Island.</p><h3><b>Will the lead plume reach Chicago?</b></h3><p>Illinois EPA officials say based on current air modeling conducted by the U.S. Army, the dust cloud from the detonation could come close to Mercer County in Illinois. It’s unclear whether the lead dust could blow as far northeast as Chicago. The Army will update its models prior and following the detonation, which could change what Illinois communities might be affected.</p><h3><b>What do we know about the health effects for people?</b></h3><p>The EPA says there is no safe level of lead exposure. It is a neurotoxin that damages the central nervous system. It’s particularly harmful to children as their brains and nervous systems aren’t fully developed. Exposure to lead is associated with cognitive delays, heart problems, and reproductive issues.</p><p>“Lead is an element, and doesn't break down,” says Robert Hirschfeld, director of water policy at the Prairie River Network, a Champaign-based environmental advocacy group.</p><p>“Those health risks persist as long as the lead does.”</p><p>As part of the controlled detonation, federal officials are installing air monitors and will conduct further environmental sampling of the blast area.</p><h3><b>Will this affect Illinois crops or animals?</b></h3><p>The agricultural impacts of the lead dust are still unknown, according to Hirschfeld. “We’re past harvest now, and so all of that lead is going to land on bare soil and that lead will stay there and contaminate that soil,” Hirschfeld says.</p><p>He says lead contamination could go beyond the potentially impacted farmland and crops, and trickle down to animals, whether livestock or wildlife, that graze on the land.</p><h3><b>What safety precautions do people exposed to the plume need to take?</b></h3><p>The Illinois Department of Public Health recommends the following safety tips:</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-4b1b1f80-e463-11f1-83d0-11b933b990fd"><li>Stay indoors and keep windows closed for 24 to 48 hours after the detonation.</li><li>If you have an HVAC system that actively draws in outside air, like a school or commercial building, then you may want to temporarily close the intake and switch to recirculate.</li><li>Use a portable air cleaner to supplement your furnace filter.</li><li>Wash outdoor surfaces when you see visible dust using soap and water.</li><li>If you need to drive through an area impacted by dust, set your car’s AC/heater to recirculate. Afterward, you can take your car to the car wash and replace the cabin filter, if needed. A high efficiency cabin filter will capture fine particulate matter.</li><li>Wash your hands before eating and drinking and take your shoes off at the entrance when you enter your home. </li><li>Visit your doctor if you have health concerns.</li></ul>

entries.title: Evanston landmark officials look to save modernist Chase bank from demolition
entries.summary: <p>Evanston's Preservation Commission voted in favor of pursuing landmark status for a modernist Chase bank branch designed by a disciple of Mies van der Rohe.</p><p>In a 9-0 vote, the commission decided the 47-year-old, one-story brick-and-glass structure by architect David Haid meets two important criteria needed for designation.</p><p>The commission's Wednesday evening decision halts JPMorgan Chase's plans to demolish the building at 1900 Central St. in favor of a new branch. The vote protects the building's exterior from demolition and unsympathetic alterations until permanent landmark status is granted.</p><p>"I hope Chase won't view this as a defeat but rather as an opportunity," said Evanston resident James McKee, who researched the building's history and recommended the structure for designation. "Chase is the custodian of an important piece of Evanston's architectural history, and I hope they'll embrace that role by restoring and improving the building while adapting the interior to meet their current needs."</p><p>The vote requires Evanston's preservation staff to create a report detailing why the bank is a unique architectural type and the work of a significant architect — two of the criteria necessary for landmark status.</p><p>That report and a draft resolution in favor of landmarking the building will be up for a vote in a commission meeting in the next few months. If approved, both documents would be sent to the Evanston City Council for a vote on whether the bank receives permanent landmark status.</p><p>During Wednesday's nearly two-hour meeting, JPMorgan Chase Vice President Kenneth Colliander and preservation consultant George Kisiel of Okrent Kisiel Associates argued against landmarking the building. Colliander, an architect, said the branch's exposed steel structure is weathered, rusted and in need of at least $3 million in repair.</p><p>Kisiel told the commission that neither the building nor Haid are distinguished enough to merit landmarking the branch.</p><p>The building "fails to be distinguished by innovation, rarity, uniqueness, or overall quality of design, detail and materials," said Kisiel, who added Haid's "body of work is limited, consists of lesser commissions that are not recognized by local or national chapters of the [American Institute of Architects]."</p><p>But commission members rejected Colliander and Kisiel's testimony and spoke glowingly about the bank's architecture and Haid's importance. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided by Jim McKee</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>"I think that the work of Mies' disciples like David Haid is important," said commission member Stuart Cohen, a preeminent architect who, in the 1970s, co-founded a group of architects nicknamed "<a class="Link" href="https://www.wttw.com/beeby/chicago-seven" target="_blank" >The Chicago Seven</a>" that challenged the dominance of architectural postmodernism. "I would make the argument that the significance of Mies' architecture and buildings like this done by people that he trained is unique."</p><p>"No one's building structures like this anymore," Cohen said of the bank. " There aren't really that many of them around, and none of them are as good as this."</p><p>Haid, who died in 1993 at age 64, studied under Mies at the Illinois Institute of Technology and worked in the famed architect's Chicago office before striking out on his own.</p><p>His Evanston bank, built in 1979 for FirstBank then later acquired by JPMorgan Chase, is part of Haid's body of work that "actively extended from his Miesian foundation — representing one of the purest, most refined expressions of the Second Chicago School [of Architecture] during the critical transitional era of Late Modernism," a report to the commission from Evanston’s Office of Historic Preservation said.</p><p>"If one strips away the brick and glass, there is a simple steel roof plane supported by four elegant columns," Evanston resident Philip Castillo, managing director at the architecture firm Jahn and supporter of the designation, told the commission. "The result is a simple, column-free interior space."</p><p>In addition to the bank, Haid's work includes the superlative Walter H. Dyett High School for the Arts, 555 E. 51st St., that he designed with Black architect Kenneth Childers; his own Evanston residence; and the Ben Rose House's auto pavilion that housed, for a while, at least, Cameron Frye’s father's red Ferrari in “Ferris Bueller’s Day Off” — Kisiel dismissively called the black steel-and-glass treasure "a garage."</p><p>Did the commission do the right thing by placing the bank on the path toward landmark designation? </p><p>It did. Although, I wish the beautiful interior could be designated also. At any rate, JPMorgan Chase has more money than Croesus and can well afford to restore the building and redevelop the branch's surface parking lot without having to shake the couch cushions for change.</p><p>After all, this is the same company that's spending $800 million to renovate Chase Tower at 10 S. Dearborn St. and shelled out $6 billion, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wsj.com/finance/banking/jpmorgans-skyscraper-on-park-avenue-estimated-to-cost-around-6-billion-76881bb3" target="_blank" >according to the Wall Street Journal</a>, to raze its 52-story 1960s headquarters in New York City and build an even taller building that opened on the site last year.</p><p>"I think Chase could turn this into something really positive," McKee said. "A source of community pride and goodwill and maybe even a way to attract some new customers through the door."</p>

entries.title: Justice Department accuses 'Broadview 6' judge of acting as a 'prosecutor,' wants mediator to step in
entries.summary: <p>The Justice Department on<b> </b>Thursday<b> </b>accused<b> </b>the<b> </b>judge<b> </b>presiding over the wreckage of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >“Broadview Six”</a> case of acting as “investigator and prosecutor,”<b> </b>arguing that a “disinterested”<b> </b>third party<b> </b>should consider whether to block testimony<b> </b>from federal prosecutors in Chicago.</p><p>Associate Attorney General <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/06/broadview-6-hearing-set-to-rock-chicago-federal-courthouse-but-doj-official-could-intervene" target="_blank" >Stanley<b> </b>Woodward</a><b> </b>made the argument<b> </b>in another court filing<b> </b>that landed on the eve of a deadline set by U.S. District Judge April<b> </b>Perry. She’s<b> </b>ordered<b> </b>U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros<b> </b>and three prosecutors who worked the “Broadview Six” case<b> </b>to testify<b> </b>Dec. 2.</p><p>But<b> </b>the Justice Department<b> </b>complained<b> </b>that<b> </b>legal privileges<b> </b>should block portions of that testimony. So<b> </b>Perry<b> </b>gave<b> </b>the three prosecutors who worked the case<b> </b>until<b> </b>Friday<b> </b>to submit a written version<b> </b>of any potentially privileged testimony<b> </b>for her review.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/16/broadview-six-andrew-boutros-stanley-woodward" >‘Broadview 6’ prosecutors say they won’t take the Fifth as potentially explosive hearing looms</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Now, Woodward has said a “special master”<b> </b>or<b> </b>some other<b> </b>“disinterested judicial officer” should<b> </b>rule<b> </b>on the Justice Department’s privilege claims.</p><p>“This court, having assumed the roles of investigator and prosecutor in addition to its native function as decisionmaker, cannot be the one to rule on the government’s privilege assertions,” Woodward argued in his four-page filing<b> </b>Thursday.</p><p>“Because this court is acting as judge and investigator,”<b> </b>he added, “it would be exceedingly difficult, if not impossible, for the court itself to decide questions of privilege while also preserving the perception of fairness.”</p><p>Woodward is the third-highest ranking official in the Justice Department, and he’s earned a reputation for tangling with federal judges. He made national headlines by facing off with U.S. District Judge Ana<b> </b>Reyes<b> </b>in Washington<b> </b>last month, over a golf course President Donald Trump has sought to renovate in the nation’s capital.</p><p>Woodward made an uneventful appearance in Perry’s courtroom Monday.</p><p>But Perry has already accused Woodward of delay tactics. She’s also denied similar requests<b> </b>in recent weeks<b> </b>as the potentially explosive Dec. 2<b> </b>hearing draws nearer. In turn,<b> </b>Woodward has floated the idea of turning to the<b> </b>7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/06/broadview-6-hearing-set-to-rock-chicago-federal-courthouse-but-doj-official-could-intervene" >Broadview 6 hearing set to rock Chicago federal courthouse, but DOJ official could intervene</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The “Broadview Six” case began as a conspiracy prosecution against six Operation Midway Blitz protesters. It <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >collapsed</a> in spectacular fashion<b> </b>in May amid allegations of prosecutor misconduct.</p><p>While the controversy initially turned on claims made against one veteran rank-and-file prosecutor, Perry has recently <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/09/feds-appear-to-hide-name-of-government-lawyer-in-new-broadview-six-court-filing" target="_blank" >raised concerns</a> about the veracity of statements<b> </b>Boutros and others<b> </b>made to her while the case played out.</p><p>The day the “Broadview Six” case fell apart, for example, Boutros told Perry he only learned of certain misconduct by his team in late April. Later, he acknowledged he’d received a transcript by email on Oct. 14, 2025, documenting the misconduct at issue.</p><p>Boutros said he didn’t remember reading it.</p><p>Separately, his team told Perry in March there were “no communications of any nature from, to, or with anyone outside [the U.S. attorney’s office] (other than the local FBI investigators assigned to the case) regarding any investigatory or charging decisions.</p><p>“To be crystal clear, this specifically includes anyone in the White House” or at Justice Department headquarters in Washington, prosecutors wrote.</p><p>Perry originally took the feds at their word that the communications don’t exist, but Boutros’ team has since suggested otherwise.</p>

entries.title: Suspect held after exchange of gunfire leaves 1 dead, 1 injured in Greater Grand Crossing
entries.summary: <p>Charges are pending for the alleged assailant who, during a shootout, killed a 46-year-old man and wounded another man early Friday in the Greater Grand Crossing neighborhood. </p><p>The men, ages 46 and 42, were outside on the 7100 block of S. Indiana Ave. when an unidentified man approached them with a gun about 12:30 a.m., police said. A brief physical altercation followed, before the men exchanged gunfire.</p><p>The 46-year-old suffered multiple gunshot wounds and was taken to University of Chicago Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead, police said. The 42-year-old was shot in the leg and was hospitalized in serious condition.</p><p>The suspected shooter fled but was quickly taken into custody, police said. A weapon was recovered, and charges are pending. </p><p>Area One detectives are investigating.</p>
entries.author: Christiana Freitag

entries.title: String of North Side shootings Wednesday and Thursday linked, says Chicago Police
entries.summary: <p>The same shooter carried out two fatal shootings, including the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/19/woman-fatally-shot-during-homicide-man-fatally-shot-in-death-investigation-overnight-in-rogers-park" target="_blank" >death of 24-year-old Bintou Salami,</a> and the attack of a 35-year-old who man was shot and robbed on a bike trail late Wednesday and early Thursday, according to Chicago police. </p><p>Police have not given a description of the alleged attacker and said no one was in custody. </p><p>The three attacks unfolded at about 10:40 p.m. Wednesday when a 35-year-old man was found shot and robbed along a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/19/man-shot-robbed-lake-view-bike-path" target="_blank" >bike path at 3300 block of North DuSable</a> Lake Shore Drive in Lake View. </p><p>Then, at 11:15 p.m., Salami was found with a fatal gunshot wound to the head outside her apartment at the 1400 block of West Chase Avenue in Rogers Park. </p><p>Salami, who recently moved to the neighborhood to be closer to her job at Misericordia Heart of Mercy, was parking a Lime scooter when someone attempted to rob her before fatally shooting her, Salami’s family told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Two hours later and about a half a mile away from Salami's murder, a still-unidentified 25-year-old man was found with a fatal gunshot wound in the stairwell of the Morse station at 1358 W. Morse Ave. An autopsy is scheduled Friday for the 25-year-old man to determine the cause and manner of his death, according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>Detectives have determined that all three incidents are connected and remain under active investigation.</p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for details.</i> </p>

entries.title: Students shouldn't rely on AI to do the heavy lifting
entries.summary: <p>As a Chicago Public Schools student, I have mixed feelings about the growing use of artificial intelligence in schools. I am not against AI entirely and think that it can be helpful when used correctly. </p><p>AI can help students brainstorm ideas or point them in the right direction when they are struggling and don't have a teacher nearby to ask questions. But I don't believe AI should do the learning for us. </p><p>One of my biggest concerns is <a class="Link" href="https://search.google/ways-to-search/ai-overviews/" target="_blank" >Google’s AI Overviews</a> feature. In school when I search for something, I'm immediately given a summarized answer, and while this may seem convenient, I think it can actually hurt students rather than help them in the long run because most students stop exploring once they see the search results. Research is more than just getting an answer. It involves reading different sources, comparing information and identifying the facts and what content is important. When an AI summary appears at the top of the page, students get answers but don’t develop the crucial skills. </p><p>For this reason, I don't have a problem with removing Google search in schools. I believe students should spend more time doing the work themselves instead of relying on AI to do it for them. If we become too dependent on AI for simple research and critical thinking, we risk raising a generation that knows how to get instant answers but does not know how to think for themselves. </p><p>Again, I think AI can be a useful tool, but it should be used to support learning rather than replace it. As technology continues to advance, schools should prioritize teaching students how to think for themselves.</p><p><i>Madison Delapaz, senior, Lane Tech College Prep</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ca0000" name="module-ca0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p><i> </i></p><h3>Criticizing Israel doesn’t equate to Jewish hate </h3><p>I appreciated the two recent thought-provoking columns on the Holocaust by Neil Steinberg — one describing his discussion with Polish poet <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/10/20/polish-poet-turns-words-of-holocaust-victims-perpetrators-into-shards-of-memory-activism" >Grzegorz Kwiatkowski </a>and another one his visit to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/11/12/anne-frank-exhibit-griffin-museum-of-science-and-industry-denialism" >Anne Frank exhibition</a> at the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry with the consul general of the Netherlands. Both columns are worth reading.</p><p>However, I take issue with Steinberg's uncalled for aside in the latter piece: "If you hate Jews — and who doesn't nowadays?"  I want to point out to Steinberg that it is possible and appropriate to hate what the state of Israel has done, and continues to do, in Gaza — utter carnage and destruction with almost 75,000 Palestinians killed. You can hate that without extending hatred toward Jewish people.</p><p><i>Blaise J. Arena, Des Plaines</i></p><h3>Cold comfort</h3><p>As winter's chill descends on thee</p><p>Two thoughts to help you cope</p><p>The North Side has the MVP</p><p>The South Side has the pope</p><p><i>Jim Vespe, Mamaroneck, New York</i></p><h3></h3>

entries.title: Trump's performative tough-on-China talk
entries.summary: <p>Don't you wish you could administer truth serum to Laura Ingraham, Steve Bannon or the dozens of other Trumpists who proclaimed their belief in Trump's "toughness" on the People's Republic of China? Remember how they used to talk? In 2019, the late Lou Dobbs opened his broadcast one night on Fox Business this way:</p><p>"For far too long Communist China has been cheating the United States on trade. President Trump has made it clear: The failure of previous presidents to aggressively represent U.S. interests in foreign policy and economic policy has ended, and President Trump made believers out of the Chinese today."</p><p>Donald Trump's rhetoric on "Chy-na" was feverish. They were waging "economic war" on us. They were "raping" our country. They were sending us the "China virus" or the "Kung Flu." Trump's supposed hawkishness on China was a selling point with working-class men. Here was a foreign scapegoat for the loss of manufacturing jobs. The focus on China justified a whole school of foreign policy advisers, led by Elbridge Colby, currently the undersecretary of defense for policy, joined by Pete Hegseth, JD Vance, Josh Hawley and Ron DeSantis, who favored limiting assistance to Ukraine in the name of keeping our powder dry for China.</p><p>What do these faux-hawks really think as they contemplate Trump's summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. That he's tough? Good God.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-570000" name="module-570000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>The West prevailed over the Communist world in the Cold War for many reasons — communism makes countries poorer, for one thing-but a key factor was our superior technology. We maintained that dominance by export controls to keep American-derived knowledge out of the hands of those who wished us ill.</p><p>We are not today in a Cold War with China, but China is the most powerful repressive country on the planet, and one whose propaganda ceaselessly agitates against the U.S. The China hawks are right to be wary of China, though wrong in just about every other way.</p><p>But Trump, hyperventilating threats notwithstanding, is not a China hawk, nor is he a dove. Those categories don't apply to him, because they imply an interest in policy and in the nation. Trump doesn't make decisions that way. His chief focus — and, frankly, his only real concern-can be found in the shaving mirror.</p><p>The Nvidia scandal (I'm referring to the Trump administration's actions, not the honey trap) is merely the capstone on the second-term pattern.</p><p>Like most bullies, Trump kisses up and punches down. As soon as someone punches back, Trump becomes a toothless crocodile. The pattern held with China. After imposing up to nearly 150% tariffs on Chinese goods on "Liberation Day," Trump found that China was not, in fact, down. It struck back with export limits on rare earths. Trump was flummoxed.</p><p>As Anja Manuel, a former State Department official, told the Wall Street Journal, China "stood up to President Trump with the rare earths, and the U.S. backed down." Trump quietly reversed several of the tariffs and then announced the result as a great "deal" after meeting with Xi.</p><p>Trump was more blase about threats from China than most members of the Republican and Democratic parties were. In 2024, large majorities of both parties voted for the Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act, a law that would require TikTok, a Chinese-owned company subject to state controls, to be sold. In his first term, Trump had labeled TikTok a grave national security threat, but when he returned to office in January 2025, he (illegally) suspended enforcement of the law. The legislators, and even the Supreme Court, thought the app was a propaganda arm of the China and had concerns about the data it was collecting from its tens of millions of American users. But Trump apparently did his usual analysis of all matters great and small: <i>Is it good for me?</i> After concluding that it was, since many Trump supporters got their news from TikTok, he declined to enforce the law and later arranged for TikTok to be sold to a consortium of Trump cronies.</p><p>Hot rhetoric notwithstanding, Trump has persistently retreated from substantive policies that would have signaled actual seriousness to China. Boasting of his "great relationship" with Xi, Trump froze a planned $14 billion arms package to Taiwan, signaled that he might lift sanctions on Chinese companies that bought Iranian oil and canceled defense talks with Taiwan. Though he didn't do it to please the Chinese strongman, Trump surely made Xi smile when he withdrew several carrier groups from the South China Sea to redeploy to the Middle East after launching his war on Iran.</p><p>On top of this pattern of laxity, the Nvidia story represents a direct betrayal of U.S. national security — one so enormous that you have to reach for fiction for analogies. A president has a mental health meltdown? A Chinese mole makes it to the Oval Office? For two years now, the world has been transfixed by the potential threat of artificial intelligence. It's practically all we talk about. Everyone in the free world understands that in the race to dominate the industry, the U.S. and China are locked in competition. Perhaps the doomers are wrong to think the fate of humanity hangs in the balance, but at least we know that it's kind of important that with a technology so powerful that it might upend everything, it's better that the Chinese Communist Party not get ahead of us.</p><p>The advanced computer chips Nvidia manufactures are key to command and control, surveillance, the generation of deepfakes and much more. That's the risk that permitting export of those chips poses for national security. What was Trump's interest? Well, Nvidia powers the AI companies that are currently driving the stock market boom. Trump has personally invested between $13 million and $62 million in Nvidia stock, and he doubtless appreciated Jensen Huang's contribution of $25 million for the White House ballroom. So when Marco Rubio and Scott Bessent, the secretaries of state and the treasury, objected that Howard Lutnick, the secretary of commerce, is not enforcing export controls on Nvidia chips, it put Trump in a tough spot. On one hand, you have national security and the need to protect America from Chinese acquisition of the most sensitive technology in the world; on the other, you have Trump's personal fortune possibly increasing through Nvidia's success in selling to everyone, China included. It's a tough choice, right?</p><p>Trump is worse than weak. He is, and has always been, for sale. We didn't need the Nvidia scandal to prove this. If there is a conflict between Trump's personal interest in vacuuming up cash and the national interest, his personal interest will prevail. Every single time.</p><p>This week's summit provided yet another opportunity for Trump to hone his "great relationships" with the world's worst dictators. It's also an opportunity for the Democrats, who will soon gain the gavels in Congress, to reflect that they are the bulwark of national security now.</p><p><i>Mona Charen is policy editor of the Bulwark and host of the “Beg to Differ” podcast.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-130000" name="module-130000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: The next 10: Illinois high school basketball teams that just missed out on the preseason Super 25 rankings
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-basketball-rankings/2026/11/17/michael-obriens-preseason-super-25-illinois-high-school-basketball-rankings" >preseason Super 25 rankings</a> are out. There will be plenty of other teams around the city and suburbs –– and, for the first time this year, throughout the state — who will join them as the season plays out.</p><p>So, no, the following teams aren’t ranked now. But these teams have the personnel and showed just enough promise during sneak peek season — also known as the month of June — to open some eyes. They hope to do more of the same this winter when it matters.</p><p>Here are 10 flying-under-the-radar sleepers to watch this winter.</p><h3><b>Buffalo Grove</b></h3><p>The Mid-Suburban League is undoubtedly a bit down this season. But don’t blame Buffalo Grove, a team that will be considerably better than last year’s 13-19 team.</p><p>Alex Sirbu, a physical 6-9 big man and rebounding machine headed to Columbia in the Ivy League, will be a force this season. He’s one of the top 10 seniors in the Class of 2027.</p><p>Then there is 7-footer Nathan Freiheit, who can finish with a dunk and step out and make a three, and returning guards Dylan Ronczkowski at point guard and Edwin Karnauchovas, a 6-2 senior who averaged 13 a game last year.</p><h3><b>Libertyville</b></h3><p>Maybe the Wildcats are a year away. But don’t discount what they could accomplish this season as a much-improved junior-dominated team. This is a team that could prove to be substantially better than its preseason profile after finishing 16-13 a year ago.</p><p>The catalyst will be junior Terrence Davis, who missed all of last season with an injury. He’s a potentially dynamic difference-maker as a 6-2 guard. Junior Nick Baker is a returning starter and joins Davis in the backcourt.</p><h3><b>Geneva</b></h3><p>The floor is high for the Vikings, thanks to a fascinating collection of guards.</p><p>Cody Rader played a significant role last season as a freshman point guard. And the Udoiwod brothers — senior David and sophomore Jonny — are talented sidekicks with legit scoring ability on the perimeter.</p><p>There isn’t much size but veteran Ben Peterson and Nelson Wendell are multi-sport senior athletes who check off many of the intangible boxes. Anything the Vikings can get from the players with size, 6-5 Owen Harrison and 6-6 junior Riggins Travieso, will be an added bonus.</p><h3><b>Crystal Lake South</b></h3><p>The Gators have three of the most valuable commodities in the sport: size, a go-to star in the backcourt and continuity.</p><p>A year after winning 27 games and reaching a sectional final, coach Matt LePage has virtually the entire team returning. That includes three All-Fox Valley Conference players, led by one of the area’s underrated players — Carson Trivellini. The 6-3 guard is the FVC’s best player after putting up 19.1 points and four assists a game last season.</p><p>Nick Stowasser, an athletic 6-5 senior guard, and 6-6 junior Ryan Morgan are two other all-league returners. Keep an eye on emerging senior Noah Cook, an intriguing 6-7 athlete who averaged 10 points a game last season.</p><h3><b>Lyons</b></h3><p>The West Suburban Silver contenders — arguably the slight favorite over York — have a talented trio to put a scare in just about anyone.</p><p>Grant Smith is one of the top 10 junior prospects and led the Lions with 17 a game last season. Point guard Timmy Sloan is a Division II recruit headed to Northern Michigan and is already the school’s all-time assist leader. And Quinn Carroll is a very promising sophomore. All three bring excellent size to the perimeter skill positions.</p><h3><b>Mount Carmel</b></h3><p>The Caravan took quite an unexpected hit this fall with the departure of DK Heard, one of the state’s best sophomores. With Heard transferring to King and some key members arriving late due to football, it might take some time for coach Phil Segroves’ team to get its bearings straight.</p><p>But make no mistake, the Caravan could very well be Super 25-worthy before it’s all said and done. Super sophomore guard Ronald Johnson and underrated 6-4 senior wing Logan Wessel are a pair of double-digit returning scorers. Football star Marshaun Thornton is terrific. And 6-10 Tim Andrele is the wild card.</p><h3><b>Young</b></h3><p>The rare year — almost unprecedented over the past two decades — where Young is absent from the preseason rankings. But the Dolphins are going to be more than competitive, particularly in the second half of the season when the youth has a little more seasoning.</p><p>CJ Pittman is a good place to start at point guard. The transfer from Payton put up 18 points and six assists a game last season as a sophomore. Look for a big jump to be made by 6-4 guard TJ Jamison, one of the top sophomore prospects in the state.</p><h3><b>Marshall</b></h3><p>Yes, we are including a Class 1A school. The Commandos are the defending state champs, but they are looking for more this season.</p><p>This should be an even better team than the one that played the likes of Rich, Simeon and Leo very tough in losses last season.</p><p>Marshall returns four of its top six players and nine players in all, including the catalyst and leading scorer from a year ago, senior guard Darrin Laye, Jr., and second leading scorer Rayvon Myles (11.5 ppg). The addition of Manley transfer Yak Kizer, a senior who provides size and rebounding at 6-5, is just what coach Darrin Laye needed.</p><h3><b>Normal</b></h3><p>It’s not very often you can include a perennial power like Normal, featuring a bonafide star and big-time winning coach, as a “sleeper.” But with the freshness of a Sun-Times Super 25 now including teams from all over the state, Normal is just that — a sleeper.</p><p>In the five years since the Covid-shortened season, coach Dave Witzig’s program has averaged 28 wins a season, including a Class 4A state runner-up finish in 2024.</p><p>Witzig, who also has a second-place finish in 2015 and fourth-place finish in 2011, lost four starters. But the Ironmen have one of the top talents in the state in 6-6 junior Chase Kasten, who averaged 17 points, 7.7 rebounds and knocked down 65 threes last season as a sophomore. He should be a dominant figure.</p><p>There are new starters and new roles for everyone. But the inexperienced players on this team did win as underclassmen.</p><h3><b>Rich </b></h3><p>All the talk in the Southland Conference is centered around Bloom. Thornwood has received a little pub as well. But don’t forget about coach Lou Adams’ Raptors.</p><p>There are a lot of unknowns with two incoming transfers and some youth, but Rich does return two key starters in 6-4 wing TJ Eaton and guard Amari Winters, a four-year varsity player.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-430000" name="html-embed-module-430000"></a><iframe title="No Shot Clock, Ep. 207: Revealing the 2026-27 statewide preseason Super 25 rankings" allowtransparency="true" height="150" width="100%" style="border: none; min-width: min(100%, 430px);height:150px;" scrolling="no" data-name="pb-iframe-player" src="https://www.podbean.com/player-v2/?i=u6iwm-1bb41bc-pb&from=pb6admin&share=1&download=1&rtl=0&fonts=Arial&skin=1&font-color=auto&logo_link=episode_page&btn-skin=c73a3a" loading="lazy"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Bears report: CB Kyler Gordon likely out Sunday
entries.summary: <p>What happened Friday at Halas Hall:</p><h3>Kyler likely out</h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson was asked Friday morning if he expected slot cornerback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/18/bears-injury-report-cb-kyler-gordon-jeffery-simmons-out-limited-nfl" target="_blank" >Kyler Gordon</a> to play Sunday against the Saints.</p><p>"Probably not," he said.</p><p>The Bears will practice later in the day and then issue an injury report for Sunday's game against the Saints at noon at Soldier Field. </p><p>Gordon hurt his shoulder before the bye week against the Buccaneers. He left the game briefly, going to the locker room, before returning and finishing the contest. Gordon did not practice with the Bears on Monday, Tuesday or Thursday. Johnson said earlier in the week that the team was treating the injury as "day-to-day," which would seemingly eliminate the possibility of putting him on injured reserve Saturday.</p><p>With Gordon out, the Bears could turn to rookie Malik Muhammad, who hasn't played since Week 7 because of a toe injury but is expected to return Sunday. He hasn't carried an injury designation this week.The team could also use safety Cam Lewis in the slot and put Elijah Hicks at safety.<br></p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Sweet shooting, chemistry-rich Evanston hopes a renewed focus on defense leads to a March trip to Champaign
entries.summary: <p>There were moments last season when Evanston’s offense achieved basketball beauty. The Wildkits hummed with unselfish passing and smooth shot-making. They finished as the highest-scoring team in the school’s long history.</p><p>The majority of the starting lineup returns for the Wildkits. Senior Vito Rocca, a 6-5 Dartmouth recruit, leads a group that includes junior guard Ben Ojala and seniors Dion Lane and Tate Schroeder.</p><p>“They can put the ball in the basket,” Evanston coach Mike Ellis said. “A lot of shooters on the floor, and they are all willing passers. I love how they share the ball. They are not guys that focus on their stats. They just want to see us play well together.”</p><p>But Ellis doesn’t want to hear anything about so many returning starters giving his team a leg up this season.</p><p>“That irks me every time I hear that,” Ellis said. “When someone says you are going to be good because you have four starters back. Every season is a new movie, a new book. I’ve seen a lot of teams that have returning starters not do as well as the previous season. And I’ve seen some return a lot and have an even greater season.”</p><p>The Wildkits finished 27-7 last year and lost to DePaul Prep in the sectional final. Expectations are sky-high this season. Evanston is No. 3 in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-basketball-rankings/2026/11/17/michael-obriens-preseason-super-25-illinois-high-school-basketball-rankings" >preseason Super 25</a> and one of the serious Class 4A state championship contenders.</p><p>“The seniors feel a responsibility, and we know we can make something special here,” Rocca said. “It starts with the seniors and works its way down the whole roster.”</p><p>And it isn’t any secret what the team needs to improve to make the season special.</p><p>“Last year was rough defensively,” Ojala said. “It is the same concepts this year, but there has to be more discipline. We need to flip the script defensively.”</p><p>“Ball pressure,” Lane said. “It comes down to the guards keeping the ball in front of them. Last year we put [Rocca] in a lot of trouble, forcing him to foul when he shouldn’t have to. That was on the guards.”</p><p>Rocca and Schroeder, a 6-5 senior, provide decent size and Maaz Dinca, a 6-7 sophomore transfer from Von Steuben, should contribute. Senior guard Dillon Pompey, a bench player last year, is expected to join the starting lineup.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-880000" name="image-880000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7bb9732/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3074x1725+0+162/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F44%2F96%2Ff111e3b94debb2bb18695cecdf86%2Fob-cst-111126-015.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3e903bb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3074x1725+0+162/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F44%2F96%2Ff111e3b94debb2bb18695cecdf86%2Fob-cst-111126-015.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2c7e13d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3074x1725+0+162/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F44%2F96%2Ff111e3b94debb2bb18695cecdf86%2Fob-cst-111126-015.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Evanston’s Ben Ojala (10) works a drill against Grayson Nangle (14) during basketball practice. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2c7e13d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3074x1725+0+162/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F44%2F96%2Ff111e3b94debb2bb18695cecdf86%2Fob-cst-111126-015.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0d41f50/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3074x1725+0+162/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F44%2F96%2Ff111e3b94debb2bb18695cecdf86%2Fob-cst-111126-015.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2c7e13d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3074x1725+0+162/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F44%2F96%2Ff111e3b94debb2bb18695cecdf86%2Fob-cst-111126-015.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Evanston’s Ben Ojala (10) works a drill against Grayson Nangle (14) during basketball practice.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kirsten Stickney/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Several young players are worth watching. Turner Schroeder, Tate’s brother, is a 6-6 sophomore. There is already some hype around 5-11 freshman guard Grayson Nangle.</p><p>“I want to have them in this element to grow their games as fast as possible, but I also want them to play, whether that is on varsity or sophomore,” Ellis said. “I told them, you will tell me what team you are on. Not me telling you.”</p><p>While there is definitely a preseason focus on team defense, don’t expect the Wildkits to slow anything down this season.</p><p>“Last year we were playing defense to get to offense instead of playing defense as our offense,” Tate Schroeder said. “We are at our best when we get stops and get in transition. Our mindset has to be to destroy them on the defensive end, and the offense will come along with it.”</p><p>Evanston returns to the Centralia Holiday Tournament this season and has major nonconference showdowns against St. Ignatius, Romeoville, Lockport, Oswego and Peoria Richwoods. The Wildkits open the season on Tuesday against Willowbrook at the Fenton Thanksgiving Tournament.</p><p>“I love the time they spend together in the gym,” Ellis said. “They do it the right way. They are all high-character student-athletes from high-character families. I don’t have to worry about off-the-court or chemistry issues at all.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-430000" name="html-embed-module-430000"></a><iframe title="No Shot Clock, Ep. 207: Revealing the 2026-27 statewide preseason Super 25 rankings" allowtransparency="true" height="150" width="100%" style="border: none; min-width: min(100%, 430px);height:150px;" scrolling="no" data-name="pb-iframe-player" src="https://www.podbean.com/player-v2/?i=u6iwm-1bb41bc-pb&from=pb6admin&share=1&download=1&rtl=0&fonts=Arial&skin=1&font-color=auto&logo_link=episode_page&btn-skin=c73a3a" loading="lazy"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Former White Sox pitcher Lance Broadway dies at age 43
entries.summary: <p>Former White Sox pitcher Lance Broadway has died at the age of 43.</p><p>Per a Dallas County Medical Examiner report, Broadway’s body was found Tuesday in the stairwell of an apartment complex in Dallas. A cause of death has yet to be determined.</p><p>The right-hander was the Sox’ first-round pick in 2005 (15th overall) out of Texas Christian University, and made his major-league debut two years later. Broad made 19 total appearances for the White Sox over parts of three seasons, before being traded to the Mets for catcher Ramon Castro in 2009. He had a 2-2 record with a 5.24 ERA in 55 career major-league innings.</p><p>After his playing days ended, Broadway had a second career as an actor, appearing in numerous small television roles in shows like “Lucifer” and “Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.” He made his feature film debut in “Olympus Has Fallen” in 2013.</p>

entries.title: Police seek gunman driving SUV who shot woman, critically injuring her on Near West Side
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for the person behind the wheel of a black SUV who opened fire, shooting a 47-year-old woman in the head and leaving her in critical condition late Thursday on the Near West Side. </p><p>A 47-year-old woman was sitting in a parked vehicle in the 1300 block of West Hastings Street about 11:55 p.m. when a gunman behind the wheel of a black SUV pulled up and shot her, police said. </p><p>She suffered a gunshot wound to the head and brought to the University of Illinois Hospital in critical condition. Police say the attacker fled the scene in an unknown direction. </p><p>No arrests have been made. </p><p>Area 3 detectives are investigating.</p>
entries.author: Christiana Freitag

entries.title: Unseasonably warm temperatures may break nearly century-old record high
entries.summary: <p>The last time it was this warm in Chicago on Nov. 20, the Shedd Aquarium and Alder Planetarium had only been open for a few months. </p><p>Nearly a century later, the projected high for Friday is expected to tie the record high of 68 degrees set in 1930 — and forecasters say there's a chance Friday's temperatures surpass the record. </p><p>"It's certainly possible, I can't rule that out," said Kevin Birk, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service. "We may eclipse that record here this afternoon." </p><p>The stretch of warmer temperatures have been driven by a warm pattern that by be influenced by a ongoing strong El Niño conditions, according to Birk. </p><p>The unseasonable warmth won't last much longer, though. Saturday's high is expected to be 68 degrees before a cold front bringing cooler temperatures and a chance of rain moves in Sunday. </p><p>"We're going to see highs back in the 40s, so that'll be the end of these abnormally warm conditions, at least for the next week." </p><p>Birk described this week's temperatures as the "upper echelon" of warmth for mid-to-late November, but autumn-like conditions will return with the cold front.</p><p>"I think we're just going to be going back to what we typically see here in Chicago for the most part," Birk said. </p>

entries.title: Illinois officials fear a toxic lead-dust plume may spread from Army site explosion in Iowa
entries.summary: <p>Gov. JB Pritzker’s top <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment" >environmental</a> official is warning that a detonation of hazardous waste at a Department of Defense site in Iowa southwest of the Quad Cities could send lead dust into the air, creating a health threat to Illinois residents.</p><p>A public notice from the federal government Monday announced that there will be an unprecedented detonation of about 5 tons of hazardous materials at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, about 80 miles southwest of the Quad Cities.</p><p>Late Thursday, the Army moved the planned explosion from Friday to Monday Nov. 23 after politicians from Iowa and Illinois asked for a delay.</p><p>“Public safety is the Army’s top priority,” acting secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in part of a statement posted on X. “This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”</p><p>The material designated to be exploded is lead azide, which is toxic. Lead azide is a chemical used in the production of bombs. The materials have to be destroyed because there's a chance they could explode if they are moved or even remain in storage, according to the Defense Department. </p><p>The explosion is expected to create a dust plume containing lead that may cross into <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois" >Illinois</a>. Lead is toxic to humans and animals. It can be particularly harmful to children with developing brains and nervous systems. Health experts say there is no safe level of lead exposure.</p><p>“As we witnessed during this summer’s wildfire season, air pollution does not respect state lines and accordingly we strongly urge the Department of Defense to conduct comprehensive post-detonation environmental sampling,” James Jennings, director of the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency, said in a statement.</p><p>That testing, he added, should include “air, soil, and surface dust testing in potentially impacted areas of Illinois.”</p><p>Jennings asked Defense officials to share the test results with the public. The Illinois EPA will be monitoring air as well. It's unclear whether the lead dust could blow as far northeast as Chicago.</p><p>The notice from the Defense Department said it would be too dangerous to attempt to move the materials.</p><div file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>While the Army has destroyed weapons and materials in the past, it has never blown up such a large amount of this particular chemical, according to a spokesperson.</p><p>"We detonate all the time, but we have not detonated lead azide at this quantity," said Lori McFate, public affairs specialist with the Army Sustainment Command in Bettendorf, Iowa.</p><p>McFate said the explosion will take place after months of planning. The procedure has received a green light from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency regional office in Kansas City. That's a different jurisdiction than the regional EPA office in Chicago, which oversees environmental protection in Illinois. </p><p>The Army is advising nearby residents in Iowa that there will be a plume carrying elevated levels of lead. It recommends either evacuating or avoiding the area or remaining indoors with windows closed until Army officials give an all-clear notice.</p><p>“There is no safe level of lead in the body, and when inhaled or swallowed, it can pose serious <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health" >health</a> risks,” Dr. Sameer Vohra, director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, said in a statement. </p><p>“Illinois residents who may be affected by the detonation can stay safe by staying indoors and keeping windows closed for 24 to 48 hours. Washing your hands prior to eating and drinking, as well as washing outdoor surfaces with soap and water are ways to minimize exposure and limit the risk of tracking toxic residue into homes," he added.</p><p>On Thursday, the environmental group Earthjustice sued to halt the planned detonation.</p><p> “Instead of keeping people safe, the Army is knowingly blanketing communities with lead and putting the burden on families to understand and mitigate the risks of the massive plume of lead dust, <br>said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau.</p><p>For more information on the detonation, visit the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant's <a class="Link" href="https://www.army.mil/asc#org-iowa-army-ammunition-plant" target="_blank" >public notice site</a>.</p>

>Drivers on South and West sides get booted more than anywhere else in city</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkyhuty-l-h/" target="_blank" >Nicole Jeanine Johnson</a></h5><p><b>Boot blues</b>: Chicago has ticketed and booted more than 283,000 vehicles from Jan. 1, 2020 to Dec. 31, 2025. Our analysis found that drivers in some parts of the South and West sides got booted at twice the citywide rate. Tickets from red-light and speed cameras were the leading violations for those drivers. The median amount owed by booted drivers was about $650. The most was more than $106,000.</p><p><b>Drivers' side</b>: Critics of the program say a combination of automated enforcement, hefty ticket prices and mounting fees can make it hard for drivers to pay their debt. That lands them on the city's boot list. Added fees they'll face for towing and impounding can also ensnare them in a debt trap. About 43,000 vehicles were booted and towed during our six-year analysis period. As of Jan. 9, more than 12,000 vehicles had not yet been returned to drivers.</p><p><b>City response</b>: In response to our findings, Mayor Brandon Johnson's administration touted its debt relief efforts, including two programs launched in April 2025 allowing businesses and drivers to settle ticket debt from the year before, minus penalties and fees. That program ended in June 2025, when 22 new speed cameras came online, resulting in 240,000 speed-camera tickets. Now, the city has circulated a 2027 revenue proposal that includes options to raise the city's towing and storage fees.</p><p><b>Bottom line</b>: The weight of the compounding costs that drivers face when they fall behind on parking and traffic tickets is heaviest in the city's Black, working-class communities.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkyhuty-l-k/" entries.title: Man who punched Jewish man, yelled 'Free Palestine' outside Ogilvie Center charged with hate crime
entries.summary: <p>A man who allegedly punched a Jewish man and yelled "Free Palestine" in September outside the Ogilvie Transportation Center in the Loop remains behind bars Friday after he was charged with a hate crime. </p><p>Joseph Haynes, 37, was arrested Sunday and charged with a hate crime and aggravated battery in a public place, Chicago police said. A judge earlier this week ordered Haynes detained. Haynes is due back at the Skokie Courthouse on Monday. </p><p>Around 8:30 p.m. Sept. 17, Haynes approached a 38-year-old Jewish man wearing a yarmulke as he was walking in the first block of North Clinton Street when Haynes approached him and asked if he was Jewish and a Zionist, prosecutors said. </p><p>The man tried to ignore Haynes, who was "persistent" in his questioning before he eventually struck the man in the lip, knocking his glasses off his face and causing him to bleed, officials said. </p><p>Haynes then allegedly ran away yelling "Free Palestine" as he held his fist up in the air, according to court records.</p><p>A nearby witness saw the attack and checked on the man, who needed three stitches for his lip afterward, prosecutors said. </p><p>The attack was captured on video and detectives were able to track Haynes' movements because of his "distinct" clothing and height, officials said. </p><p>Haynes was seen onboard a CTA train after the attack and was identified through video by the victim and witness, court records show. </p><p>Haynes, of the Lincoln Square neighborhood, has pending cases for attempted robbery of a transit employee and aggravated battery of a transit employee, prosecutors said. </p>

entries.title: Hombre que chocó vehículo de la Patrulla Fronteriza en Chicago no irá a prisión
entries.summary: <p>Una jueza federal el jueves impuso una sentencia de tiempo cumplido a un hombre de Chicago que pasó aproximadamente cuatro días en custodia después de que condujera una camioneta Ford contra un vehículo de la Oficina de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza (CBP) durante el Operativo Midway Blitz.</p><p>La jueza federal de distrito, LaShonda Hunt, imputó la sentencia a Anthony González Álvarez, quien se declaró culpable en agosto de interferir por la fuerza con agentes de CBP, un delito menor. Álvarez es una de dos personas condenadas por un delito vinculado a la campaña de deportaciones, el Operativo Midway Blitz.</p><p>Durante la audiencia del jueves, la jueza coincidió con un fiscal que calificó la conducta de Álvarez de “imprudente y peligrosa”. Pero Hunt reconoció que Álvarez ya había pasado tiempo tras las rejas, que ha tenido pocos problemas desde su arresto y que se ha comprometido a pagar $1,362 en restitución.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-990000" name="module-990000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Antes de conocer su sentencia, Álvarez dijo, “Me arrepiento de lo que hice. De verdad. Sólo quiero disculparme y seguir con mi vida”.</p><p>Los fiscales federales en Chicago imputaron a 33 acusados conocidos por delitos vinculados al Operativo Midway Blitz. Pero se han retirado los cargos contra 28 de esas personas.</p><p>Hasta ahora, la única otra persona condenada por un delito relacionado con el operativo es Héctor Gómez. Fue sentenciado a 30 meses de prisión tras admitir que disparó un arma cerca de agentes de inmigración.</p><p>Mientras tanto, los fiscales federales están bajo escrutinio por presunta mala conducta en un caso fallido presentado contra un grupo de manifestantes de Midway Blitz conocidos como los “Broadview Six”.</p><p>Álvarez admitió en agosto que, el 3 de octubre de 2025, él se unió a una caravana de vehículos mientras conducía una camioneta Ford negra en persecución de un vehículo de CBP. El conductor del vehículo de CBP intentó alejarse de la caravana, incluso entrando en el carril equivocado del tráfico, según los registros.</p><p>Pero Álvarez lo siguió en su camioneta y, finalmente, chocó contra la parte trasera del lado del pasajero, según el acuerdo de culpabilidad de Álvarez. Álvarez ha negado haber chocado el vehículo de la CBP a propósito.</p><p>La fiscal federal adjunta Stephanie Stern señaló que, más tarde ese mismo día, Alvarez fue a una estación de policía para denunciar que su camioneta había sido robada esa mañana. Luego, por la noche, llamó al 911 para decir a la policía que había encontrado su camioneta usando un dispositivo de rastreo.</p><p>Ese no fue el primer roce de Álvarez con la ley, señaló Stern en una presentación ante la corte. Álvarez se declaró culpable en 2017 de resistirse a un agente de policía en un incidente en el que, según Stern, Álvarez le escupió a un agente.</p><p>Luego, en 2019, se declaró culpable de intento de suplantación falsa de un agente de la ley, según la fiscal. Ella escribió que se le acusó de usar luces intermitentes blancas y azules —similares a las del Departamento de Policía de Chicago— para obligar a otros vehículos a detenerse.</p><p>Finalmente, Stern le dijo a la jueza que Álvarez fue condenado en 2021 por un informe falso. Álvarez había llamado al 911 para denunciar que su hija había sido secuestrada, escribió. Pero resultó que la niña estuvo con su madre todo el tiempo, explicó Stern.</p><p>Ricardo Meza, el abogado defensor de Álvarez, reconoció la conducta ilícita de su cliente el jueves. Pero le recordó a la jueza que pocas cosas ocurren en el vacío. Y el encuentro de Álvarez con el vehículo de la CBP ocurrió en medio de una agresiva campaña de deportaciones.</p><p>“Desafortunadamente, durante el curso de ese operativo, mucha gente resultó herida”, dijo Meza. “Algunas personas incluso perdieron la vida”.</p><p>Todo eso “avivó la ira” en Álvarez, dijo, quien “no debería haber estado ahí.”</p><p>“Él siente arrepentimiento por lo que ha hecho”, le dijo Meza a la jueza. “Está listo para seguir con su vida”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Brady Pettigrew, the state's biggest high school basketball star, is focused on a state title for Bolingbrook
entries.summary: <p>Bolingbrook is now an established state power, regularly appearing near the top of the rankings and churning out high-profile stars like current Arkansas guard Davion Thompson, the 2025 Sun-Times Player of the Year who skipped his senior year of high school.</p><p>Brady Pettigrew is the latest high-level talent for Raiders’ coach Rob Brost. Pettigrew exploded on the national scene over the summer and is now widely considered a top 10 player in the national class of 2028.</p><p>One thing Bolingbrook doesn’t have is a boys basketball state championship. Pettigrew believes this is the year. The Raiders open the season at No. 4 in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-basketball-rankings/2026/11/17/michael-obriens-preseason-super-25-illinois-high-school-basketball-rankings" >preseason Super 25</a>. </p><p>“100 percent,” Pettigrew said. “Everyone is on the same page: the teachers, the fans, the managers, the coaches, the players. We are all striving for that end goal because it has never been done here and we all feel this is the year it can be done. We believe in ourselves.”</p><p>The Raiders are deep and tall and talented, but it is a new group of players still finding its way together on the court.</p><p>“We hang a lot off the court and have really good chemistry, so in that way it feels like we have been together for three years or something,” Pettigrew said. “Everyone is very mature and has the same goals.”</p><p>Isaiah Rogers, a 6-4 senior who was injured for much of last season, returns along with junior guards Mason and Marlon Williams. Nate Woods, a 6-6 senior, transferred from Lyons and Curtis Stubbs, a 6-6 senior, transferred from Providence. Six-foot-five junior Dereon Smothers spent time at TF North, Butler and a prep school and is now at Bolingbrook.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson's straight talk changes the conversation at Halas Hall
entries.summary: <p>One of the surest signs that Ben Johnson is the right coach for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> and can take them where they want to go is his willingness to acknowledge problems.</p><p>Whereas Matt Eberflus and Matt Nagy before him constantly tried to spin situations and persuade everyone messes weren’t as bad as they looked, Johnson has no hesitation calling out issues regardless of how well things are going. And he usually starts with himself.</p><p>It’s objective and straightforward, and the public was begging for it.</p><p>He was at it again this week even as his team stands 7-2 and is a consensus top-five favorite to win the Super Bowl going into a home game Sunday against the Saints. Johnson wasn’t nitpicking — he highlighted positives, too — but he readily revealed deficiencies he wants to correct.</p><p>Coaches typically are direct about those things behind the scenes, but Johnson does it when talking to the media — and, by extension, fans — in a way that Eberflus and Nagy were afraid to.</p><p>“I see talking to you the same as talking to the team and talking to the fans,” Johnson said before practice Friday. “Everybody hears everything this day in age. Whatever message is going on in the building is going to be consistent with you guys as well.</p><p>“I don't know any other way. I just try to be truthful.”</p><p>He promised “bluntness and honesty” in an interview with the Sun-Times going into his first season and has delivered.</p><p>That has its limits, of course.</p><p>In that same conversation Friday, Johnson gave the shortest possible answers about Kyler Gordon’s injury, grew annoyed by ensuing injury questions and declined to elaborate on coaching points his staff has emphasized in trying to generate more interceptions. But those areas can reasonably fall under competitive advantage, and he’s justified in keeping some specifics to himself.</p><p>When it comes to the big picture, though, Johnson’s transparency earns him credibility.</p><p>As the Bears plunged through prolonged losing streaks over the years before his arrival, coaches exasperatingly told the public it wasn’t as dire as it seemed: Things were getting better, even if you weren’t smart enough to see that. Trust us.</p><p>How’d that turn out?</p><p>This couldn’t be more different. Reporters don’t walk into Halas Hall bracing for excuses and alternative realities anymore.</p><p>You have worries? So does Johnson. The red-zone stumbles, fumbling trouble, the rushing attack stalling at points, penalties on special teams, a little too much pressure being allowed in the pocket — it’s refreshing to hear a coach call out the same concerns you have. It reassures you that they’re being addressed.</p><p>One of his main focuses this week has been identifying inefficiencies in the running game, for example.</p><p>It’s No. 4 in the league, by the way, which on the surface should be satisfying, but Johnson graded it subpar because it hasn’t met his success metrics: one-third of the distance to go on first downs, half the distance remaining on second downs and conversions on third and fourth downs.</p><p>His bar is hitting those checkpoints 55% of the time, but said the Bears are below 50%.</p><p>“Our coaches are hammering our guys,” he said at the end of his critique. “They're probably already tired of hearing about it.”</p><p>That’s how this building functions under Johnson. He insists that there’s always something to fix, even as the Bears enjoy arguably their highest approval rating in two decades. That’s going to make him a lot more believable if they ever go into a rut, which hasn’t happened yet for him at 18-8 overall.</p><p>His unrelenting push to hold the Bears to championship standards had been missing. He started in on that publicly after just two games last season, ripping the team for poor practice habits, and that sparked change.</p><p>“Beating around the bush never really gets you anything,” said right guard Jonah Jackson, whose history with Johnson goes back to the Lions. “He’s not a [jerk]. He’ll love you up. But you need to get the point across in this business to make things happen.</p><p>“You want people in your life to get straight to the point, don’t you? I assume that’s what the fans want from him, too.”</p><p>Johnson hasn’t been part of a Super Bowl coaching staff, so it’s a safe assumption that his definition of “championship-caliber” performance is to be as close to perfect as possible. And since it’ll never actually be perfect, so there will always be work to do.</p><p>That’s the essence of the culture he has established, and it echoes from key players like <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a> and D’Andre Swift. It’s the only way to grow.</p><p>Johnson is so resolute in that belief and confident in the path he’s charting that he isn’t threatened or pressured by the world knowing that his team still needs improvement if it’s going come out on top of the NFL’s toughest division and topple contenders like the 49ers, Bills and Jaguars.</p><p>There’s never a whiff of insecurity with him, leaving no need for him to try to steer public opinion in his favor. This is how serious coaches talk.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Next step for Bears DBs: take the ball away
entries.summary: <p>Jaylon Johnson’s 67-yard pick-six against the Buccaneers was as important a development for the embattled cornerback as it was the rest of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ defensive backs.</p><p>“We need more turnovers,” Johnson said. “Especially I would say as a DB group, we’ve got to get more turnovers.”</p><p>Taking the ball away has been a focus all week heading into Sunday’s home game against the Saints. If the Bears are going to beat the Saints — much less the elite teams left on their schedule: the Bills, Jaguars, Vikings, Packers and Lions — their defense needs to be more dangerous.</p><p>Landing defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons was a critical first step — the Bears’ pass rush went from a weakness to a strength. </p><p>Now the Bears’ defensive backs need to take advantage of the pressure their defensive line causes.</p><p>“He’s very disruptive,” Johnson said. “And all DBs love disruptive fronts.”</p><p>Before the Bears’ win against the Bucs, Bears cornerbacks and safeties had totaled just two interceptions all season. Then they posted two more against Baker Mayfield — Johnson’s touchdown and safety Cam Lewis’ second-quarter pick.</p><p>All told, the team has just seven this season.</p><p>The Bears didn’t have a single interception in Weeks 6-8. Four Bears DBs have one interception apiece —Malik Muhammad in Week 1 and fellow rookie Dillon Thieneman off backup Andy Dalton in Week 3, and the two against the Buccaneers.</p><p>The Bears are one of 10 NFL teams without a defensive back with at least two interceptions. The Vikings and Bucs, by contrast, boast three DBs with at least two interceptions.</p><p>“We are extremely ball-conscious …” coach Ben Johnson said. “Throughout this week we’ve taken it to another level as a coaching staff. Our guys are aware of it, and when those opportunities come our way, just making sure we capitalize on it.”</p><p>The Bears have a -4 turnover margin, tied for the sixth-worst mark in the NFL.</p><p>“That's just not winning football,” Johnson said.</p><p>With slot cornerback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/18/bears-injury-report-cb-kyler-gordon-jeffery-simmons-out-limited-nfl" target="_blank" >Kyler Gordon out Sunday</a>, defensive coordinator Dennis Allen will have to get creative. He could use Lewis, the starting safety, in the slot on passing downs — or could play Muhammad there full-time. Muhammad will appear in his first game since hurting his toe Week 7.</p><p>The Bears have been thrilled with Lewis’ versatility dating to training camp, when they had to scramble to replace injured safety Coby Bryant. Allen said such role players are key to a championship-level team. Still, they need their stars to play like it — and Johnson is making $24.5 million, the highest cap hit on the team.</p><p>Johnson has given up 30 passing yards or fewer in three of his last four games, according to NFL Next Gen Stats, after doing it just once in the Bears’ first five games. He’ll have a chance to continue that Sunday against Tyler Shough. Only seven quarterbacks have more interceptions than the Saints quarterback, who threw six in nine starts last year.</p><p>Allen hopes Johnson’s pick-six in his last game serves as a springboard.</p><p>“It's a tough league that we're in — you’ve just got to keep going out there and keep working and keep competing, and that's what he's done. …” Allen said. “I think we were all excited to see that, and I'm anticipating more of that to come.”</p>
