entries.title: In college football, "best" doesn't really mean best and clarity is just a pipe dream
entries.summary: <p>On a media conference call this week, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >College Football</a> Playoff selection committee chairman Hunter Yurachek said the margins between the “six or seven” teams following No. 1 Georgia and No. 2 Utah in the rankings are “razor thin.”</p><p>As for the top two, though, there is no doubt in the committee room.</p><p>“I think we’ve got a pretty clear understanding [about that],” Yurachek said.</p><p>If only.</p><p>CFP decision-making — since the start in 2014 — has never been clear enough. And the bigger the playoff gets — the field will double from 12 to 24 next season — the easier it’ll be to punch holes in any committee theory.</p><p>Take Utah, a Power 4 team that, based on its 10-0 record, has an obvious case for prime seeding in the playoff. But the committee’s own marching order is to seed teams in order of “best,” not “most deserving,” and this is where being completely honest about the Utes becomes next to impossible.</p><p>I asked oddsmakers at BetOnline Sports & Casino how many teams would be favored today, on a neutral field, to beat the Utes, and the answer was — get ready for this — 10. The list includes one-loss Georgia, Notre Dame (No. 6 in the CFP rankings), Miami (7) and Indiana (8); two-loss Alabama (3), Texas (5) and Tennessee (9); three-loss Oregon (13) and Ohio State (14) and, hilariously, four-loss LSU (unranked). Notably, the list does not include No. 4-ranked UCLA, the only unbeaten team aside from the Utes.</p><p>If it isn’t “razor thin” between Utah and, say, Alabama and Notre Dame, the real truth is it’s because nobody would expect the Utes to win against either of those opponents. Ah, well.</p><p>Does it make clear sense that 9-1 Indiana, the defending national champion, sits behind five teams that have lost one or two games? Or that 9-1 Wake Forest, whose lone loss was to Miami and which has won its last five ACC games by a combined score of 236-38, is down at No. 11? Or that 8-2 Iowa, playing its best football as Thanksgiving nears, is at No. 15, behind three-loss Big Ten brethren Oregon and Ohio State?</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">November 1️⃣7️⃣ <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/CFP?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#CFP</a> Top 25 🏆 <a href="https://t.co/Y03MIEWeng">pic.twitter.com/Y03MIEWeng</a></p>— CFP (@CFBPlayoff) <a href="https://x.com/CFBPlayoff/status/2122887114161529231?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Nah, not clear. It’s all just a mishmash of “data points,” guesswork and biases, and not necessarily in that order.</p><p>“This continues to be a season defined by parity,” Yurachek said, “and that’s great for the sport.”</p><p>Bah, humbug. Let me just get a few of my own opinions on record: Georgia is better than everybody else, and it isn’t all that close. Notre Dame against anybody else would be at worst a coin flip for the Irish. Once the playoff arrives, there will be more teams that can’t win it than teams that can win it — and the numbers will only get much worse in the “can’t” department when the field expands to 24.</p><p>Isn’t this fun? But let’s move on.</p><p><b>Week 12 picks</b></p><p><i>All games are Saturday. My picks to cover are listed first, with CFP rankings in effect.</i></p><p><b>Minnesota (+2½) vs. Northwestern </b>(11 a.m., FS1, 720-AM): The Gophers’ lone Big Ten loss at home the last two seasons was to UCLA this year, and Northwestern is no UCLA. The Wildcats haven’t won — or been close to winning — since quarterback Aidan Chiles got hurt. Can either team get to 20 points? That might more than get the job done. Gophers, 20-16.</p><p><b>No. 14 Ohio State (-3½) at Nebraska </b>(11 a.m., Fox 32): ESPN’s Playoff Predictor gives the Buckeyes merely a 42% chance to make the field. That’s not great, but it beats the Huskers’ 97.4% chance of screwing things up whenever humanly possible. Buckeyes, 23-17.</p><p><b>No. 8 Indiana (-7½) at Washington </b>(2:30 p.m., Peacock): No coach is feeling more disrespected these days than the Hoosiers’ Curt Cignetti. I wouldn’t want to be the Huskies right now. IU, 31-13.</p><p><b>No. 6 Notre Dame (-20½) vs. SMU </b>(6:30 p.m., NBC 5, 780-AM): How does SMU pick up the pieces one week after getting obliterated 49-7 on its home field by Wake Forest? It won’t take much for more Mustang doubt to creep in. Irish, 38-14.</p><p><b>No. 2 Utah (-7) at TCU </b>(8 p.m., Fox 32): Can the Utes win all the marbles this season? Not a chance. Can they keep the ball rolling against the 5-5 Horned Frogs. If not — sheesh — what are we even doing here? Utes by eight.</p><p>My favorite favorite: <b>No. 15 Iowa (-8½) at Illinois </b>(1:30 p.m., BTN, 890-AM): Can the Illini get a seventh win while knocking coach Bret Bielema’s alma mater out of the playoff picture? In a word, no. Well, not if quarterback Aidan Houser can’t go, and he was still in concussion protocol as of late Friday morning.</p><p>My favorite underdog: <b>Michigan (+4) vs. No. 4 UCLA </b>(2:30 p.m., Ch. 2): The weirdest thing that could happen Saturday would be for Kyle Whittingham to knock off a top-five opponent in one of his last acts as the 5-5 Wolverines’ one-and-done coach. Which means it simply must happen.</p><p><b>Last week: </b>4-3 straight-up, 3-4 against the spread.</p><p><b>Season to date: </b>56-24 straight-up, 47-33 against the spread.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/18/chicago-bears-offensive-line-darnell-wright-jonah-jackson-joe-thuney-caleb-williams-kyle-monangai-ben-johnson-new-orleans-saints" target="_blank" >Let the Bears’ offensive line — the Monsters of the Midsection — lead the way</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Chicago parks board accused of tying next mayor's hands by extending Supt. Ramirez-Rosa's contract
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Park District Board was accused Friday of tying the hands of a new mayor, if there is one, by granting Superintendent and CEO <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/02/28/ramirez-rosa-new-superintendent-park-district-rosa-escareno-retiring" >Carlos Ramirez-Rosa</a> a three-year contract extension until Dec. 31, 2029.</p><p>Ald. Nick Sposato (38th), chair of the City Council’s Committee Special Events, Cultural Affairs and Recreation, argued that it is “highly inappropriate” for the seven-member board handpicked by Mayor Brandon Johnson to give Ramirez-Rosa three more years of job security when Johnson’s own political future is undecided.</p><p>Ramirez-Rosa’s original contract was due to expire on April 30, 2027 — after both rounds of the upcoming mayoral election.</p><p>The three-year-extension, unanimously approved at the October board meeting, gives Ramirez-Rosa the post until the second half of the new mayoral term. His current salary is $260,590 after receiving the same 3% raise granted to the Park District’s unionized employees.</p><p>“Is that fair to [saddle] the mayor with somebody who maybe they’re not happy with? With the possibility of a new mayor coming in, I think it’s highly inappropriate," Sposato said. “With the uncertainty... and the very strong possibility of a new mayor, I’m surprised and disappointed with the Park District board to do something like that.”</p><p>Former 24th Ward alderman-turned-Cook County Commissioner Michael Scott Jr. spent 12 years as a Park District supervisor and area manager. He once dreamed of becoming superintendent. Although he believes Ramirez-Rosa is “doing a wonderful job," Scott criticized the contract extension.</p><p>Also critical of the move were retiring Ald. Matt O’Shea (19th); Ald. Jeanette Taylor (20th), a Johnson ally, and Ald. Emma Mitts (37th), who is among a handful of City Council members who have endorsed Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias for mayor against Johnson.</p><p>“When new administrations come in, there’s a new direction… I don’t think you should tie any mayor’s hands as they come in the door to go in a different direction," Scott said.</p><p>Ramirez-Rosa told the Sun-Times he earned the extension after a performance evaluation mandated by his first contract concluded he was "exceeding expectation."</p><p>"The board also engaged in a conversation about our five-year strategic plan that runs through Dec. 31 of 2029 and determined that, based upon my performance and based upon the needs of the organization, that it would be appropriate to extend my current contract to align with the five-year strategic plan,” Ramirez-Rosa said Friday.</p><p>He said that Chicago Housing Authority CEO Keith Pettigrew and Chicago Public Schools CEO Macquline King have multi-year contracts that extend several years into the future.</p><p>Scott and O’Shea rejected the comparison. The Park District superintendent’s job has long been a “political appointment,” they said. The CHA and CPS jobs were filled with housing and education professionals after nationwide searches, they said.</p><p>In February, 2023, Ramirez-Rosa resigned as chair of the City Council’s Zoning Committee and as Johnson’s City Council floor leader days after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2024/05/22/city-council-committee-chairs-johnson-ramirez-rosa-mitts-apology" >being accused</a> of “manhandling” Mitts, the Council’s longest-serving Black woman.</p><p>At the time, political tensions between Black and Hispanic residents were running high because of the migrant crisis that ultimately cost Chicago taxpayers $639.6 million.</p><p> Ramirez-Rosa had been accused of threatening a colleague and blocking Mitts in an attempt to prevent her from entering a special City Council meeting called in an attempt to approve an advisory referendum asking Chicago voters whether Chicago should remain a sanctuary city.</p><p>The Park District job has allowed Ramirez-Rosa to chart a new career path by improving security and bolstering programming, even as he acknowledges the ongoing struggle with 60 homeless encampments in Chicago parks.</p><p>“The Park District clearly had a problem with safety and security and he brought in Chris Kennedy, who’s really done a nice job and had a strong track record with the Chicago Police Department,” O’Shea said.</p><p>“On the other hand, the mayor’s office is making sure that their allies are getting new projects… Who’s getting park [field]houses? Park superintendents are supposed to be looking after all 77 communities where there are needs.”</p><p>Taylor said Ramirez-Rosa has “turned around some stuff, but the jury is still out.”</p><p>“I’ve gotten what I needed from the Park District. But the Park District needs a revamp if we’re being honest. We need programming where young people are actually running to the Park District — not running away from it. We can’t do what we’ve been doing forever,” Taylor said.</p><p>A similar contract extension was granted to then-Park District Supt. Mike Kelly during the closing months of then-Mayor Rahm Emanuel's administration, only to be rescinded after the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/2/18/18398890/rahm-s-agency-heads-could-outlast-him-thanks-to-golden-parachute-contracts" >Sun-Times reported</a> on the extension. </p>

entries.title: Previewing the top IHSA football semifinal playoff games
entries.summary: <h3>Class 8A: No. 4 Oswego at No. 2 Mount Carmel, 3 p.m. Saturday</h3><p>This is a rematch of last year's 8A final, won 20-3 by Mount Carmel. Oswego (11-1) avenged its only loss of the season by beating Bolingbrook 31-7 in the quarterfinals. Ammar Banire's return from injury has energized the Panthers' running game and dual-threat quarterback Drew Kleinhans has elevated his play in the postseason. Mount Carme (10-2), which is seeking its second straight 8A title and fifth in a row overall, has hit another gear after losing to Brother Rice in Week 6. Brady Cloherty has passed for 3,273 yards and a program-record 48 TDs. Marshaun Thornton, Quentin Burrell (Michigan) and Ty Kennedy all have 10 or more receiving scores.</p><p></p><h3>Class 8A: No. 3 St. Ignatius at No. 11 New Trier, 6 p.m. Saturday</h3><p>Between them, St. Ignatius (10-2) and New Trier (11-1) have two combined semifinal appearances and one title-game berth: the Trevians' runner-up finish in 6A (then the largest class) in 1982. St. Ignatius' triple-option attack, led by quarterback Reid Hites, has caused opposing defenses fits all season and helped the Wolfpack oust traditional powers Maine South and Loyola the past two weeks. New Trier has elite playmakers in the passing game and running game with Purdue-bound quarterback Jackie Ryder and Throy Nightengale, who ran for 309 yards and five TDs last week against Huntley.</p><h3>Class 7A: East St. Louis at No. 1 Brother Rice, 2 p.m. Saturday</h3><p>East St. Louis (11-1) lost star running back Myson Johnson-Cook, an Auburn commit, to injury in a season-opening win against Mount Carmel. But the Flyers have kept rolling, losing only in overtime to Florida power American Heritage. Senior quarterback Reece Shanklin (East Tennessee State) has passed for 2,904 yards and 35 touchdowns with two interceptions, while four-star Cincinnati commit Ronnie Gomiller has 1,709 total yards and 29 TDs. Brother Rice (10-2) has won eight in a row behind a dominant defense anchored by lineman Brayden Parks (Notre Dame) and Kameron McGee and an offense led by freshman quarterback Sam Holcomb (1,615 passing yards, 25 TDs, no interceptions) and running back Jameson Davis (Army).</p><p></p><h3>Class 7A: No. 9 Downers Grove North at No. 5 Hersey, 4:30 p.m. Saturday</h3><p>It's a classic unstoppable offense vs. immovable defense matchup. For Hersey (12-0), quarterback Jake Nawrot (Kentucky) has had one of the best two-year runs of any quarterback in recent memory. Over the past two seasons, he's thrown for 82 touchdowns and more than 6,100 yards with only two interceptions while completing more than 70% of his passes. Sophomore running back Jackson Travis has run for 1,584 yards and 19 TDs, while Jaxon St. Paul and Josh Riggs have combined for 31 receiving scores. Downers North (11-1) has four shutouts and hadn't allowed more than 14 points until last week's 47-29 win vs. Richards.</p><h3>Class 6A: No. 13 Nazareth at No. 15 Wheaton-Warrenville South, 1 p.m. Saturday</h3><p>Nazareth (8-5) is trying to become the second five-loss team to win state three years after becoming the first to do it. The return from injury of edge rusher Chris Kasky (Missouri) has given the Roadrunners' defense a shot in the arm. Quarterback JJ Chapman, receiver Jackson Flickinger and running back Charles Calhoun are playmakers on offense. Wheaton-Warrenville South (9-3) is back in the semifinals for the first time since finishing second in 7A in 2010. Standout quarterback AJ Rogers left last week's win against Normal West with an injury and was replaced behind center by junior receiver Steven Harvey.<br></p>

entries.title: Blackhawks dodged bullet with reportedly nixed Rickard Rakell trade
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> general manager Kyle Davidson needs to shift mindsets in the wake of Connor Bedard's latest shoulder <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/19/blackhawks-connor-bedard-injury-surgery-rehab-decision" >injury</a>.</p><p>This Hawks season is toast. That needs to be acknowledged. That's not to say it's pointless — it will still be important for individual development purposes — but the team clearly isn't going to end up anywhere close to a playoff spot.</p><p>That means Davidson's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/11/blackhawks-kyle-davidson-trades-mark-eaton-jeff-blashill" >activity</a> on the trade market must pivot away from seeking short- to medium-term help. Only younger players who could legitimately be long-term building blocks should be considered.</p><p>Per numerous <a class="Link" href="https://www.tsn.ca/nhl/article/potential-penguins-blackhawks-trade-foiled-by-rakells-no-trade-list/" target="_blank" >reports</a>, Davidson almost sprung a major trade recently for 33-year-old Penguins winger Rickard Rakell. It didn't happen because the Hawks are reportedly one of eight teams on Rakell's no-trade list and he refused to waive that clause.</p><p>In retrospect, that was a bullet dodged for the Hawks.</p><p>Rakell is a solid top-six player who would've doubtlessly improved the Hawks' current roster. He racked up 70 points two seasons ago, produced at a 66-point pace last season and has heated up to get back to a 52-point pace this season (13 points in 21 games so far) after a slow start.</p><p>But he has just one year left on his contract after this season and is at an age where decline is likely imminent. He wouldn't have been a long-term building block. </p><p>And especially sans Bedard, he's nowhere near elite enough to have dramatically changed the course of this Hawks season. He would've been a waste of a big splash.</p><p>It's unclear exactly what the Hawks were planning to give up in the nixed trade, but presumably either the Panthers' or Oilers' 2027 first-round pick — both of which they own — was involved. A prospect likely was, too. It would've been a significant package.</p><p>The Hawks indeed have such a surplus of picks and prospects that finding ways to trade them for NHL players should be a top priority moving forward. However, those picks and prospects can't be wasted, and those NHL players need to fit a certain type.</p><p>As frustrating as the start of Bowen Byram's Hawks tenure has been, he does exemplify that type as a 25-year-old theoretically just entering his prime. At this point, Davidson needs to seek out more Byrams and fewer Rakells.</p><p>Those first-round picks will probably be more valuable closer to the draft, too. That's often how it goes.</p><p>One challenge for the Hawks — and it's not a new one — is that very few other NHL franchises are rebuilding right now. Therefore, very few are interested in trading established players for picks and prospects. </p><p>The skyrocketing salary cap isn't forcing anybody to blow things up, and teams might be viewing the Hawks' lack of progress as a cautionary tale about the very concept of rebuilding. It all adds up to an extreme, inelastic sellers' market that's making Davidson's quest for talent even harder.</p><p>The Penguins, though, are one of the few teams about to enter a rebuild — or at least a retool — so they could remain intriguing trade partners for the Hawks, even beyond Rakell.</p><p>Penguins GM Kyle Dubas has been transparent about the major roster turnover ahead with the team sitting last in the Eastern Conference at 7-12-2 and cornerstone stars Sidney Crosby, Evgeni Malkin and Erik Karlsson all in the final years of their contracts.</p><p>Meanwhile, the Red Wings and Flyers are drama-laden messes, the Maple Leafs and Kings are old and bad but haven't given up yet, the Predators and Jets are old and mediocre but hanging on all right for now and the Blue Jackets and Kraken are permanently stuck in no man's land. </p><p>None have yet joined the Canucks and Flames, however, in the truly rebuilding club. </p><p>Coincidentally, the Hawks will attempt to finally earn their first road win(s) this weekend against those two foes.</p>

entries.title: Saints game is crucial for Bears QB Caleb Williams to get back on track as tougher defenses loom
entries.summary: <p>After a string of high-pressure, prime-time games for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>, their return to Soldier Field for a fairly nondescript noon kickoff against the Saints feels a little quiet.</p><p>The Bears are just a few weeks removed from knocking off the defending champion Seahawks and a few days away from visiting the division-leading Lions on Thanksgiving. In between, this might seem to be just another game.</p><p>That’s not the case at all for quarterback Caleb Williams.</p><p>This one matters quite a bit coming off an ugly, four-interception game against the Buccaneers that the Bears were “grateful” to win, as coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/20/bears-coach-ben-johnsons-straight-talk-changes-the-conversation-at-halas-hall" >Ben Johnson</a> put it. In a sharp departure following the best three-game stretch of his young career, Williams went off track with bad decisions on his way to completing just 59.5% of his passes and posting a 61.5 passer rating.</p><p>He needs to bury that one, and the Saints offer a great opportunity to do so.</p><p>Their defense, which ranks No. 29 overall, is the biggest reason they’re 3-6. They have the third-lowest pressure rate at 19.7% and have allowed the 10th-highest passer rating at 97.2. They have four interceptions, which is fifth-fewest.</p><p>Oh yeah, and starting safety Justin Reid just asked to be released.</p><p>Bottom line: This likely is the worst defense the Bears will face all season, and Williams must treat it as such.</p><p>It’s reasonable to cut Williams a break on the four picks because that’s rarely been an issue for him. Since entering the NFL in 2024, he has thrown interceptions on a league-low 1.4% of his passes. The Bucs game was definitively an aberration in that regard.</p><p>The overall lack of sharpness was the much more significant concern, and that’s the one Williams needs to put to rest.</p><p>After a hot start, he seemed to get too loose and carefree, and while Johnson doesn’t want to scrub his phenomenal improvisational skills out of his game, that style of play only got him so far.</p><p>In the season opener, Williams looked like a completely different quarterback than the one who went up and down over his first two seasons.</p><p>He showed an undeniably deeper understanding of Johnson’s offense and how to operate it ruthlessly it with quicker reads, better timing, more accurate passes and more discipline in staying in the pocket and keeping the play in its intended rhythm.</p><p>That’s what worked in dominant performances against the Falcons, Patriots and Seahawks, too, and sent Williams surging into the MVP race. He veered from that in the Bucs game.</p><p>Johnson never glosses over anything and he picked apart Williams’ interceptions in detail privately and publicly, but when asked leading up the Saints game about the totality of Williams’ first half of the season, he scored high.</p><p>“He's playing fast right,” Johnson said. “He's got a great approach. He's doing a good job downloading the game plan. We don't feel like we're hindered in any way as a coaching staff from what we're able to put in.</p><p>“He's just able to digest a lot more, and he's seeing coverage really well. We're really encouraged with where he's at. We've just got to continue to push that and see how far it'll take us.”</p><p>That’s way different from last season, when Johnson said during training camp there was a substantial gap between the offense he ran in his final season with Lions quarterback Jared Goff and the scaled-down version Williams and the Bears could handle at the beginning of his tenure.</p><p>The idea is not to turn Williams into a robot, or even for him to play like Goff. Williams brings a unique skillset to the table, and Johnson’s goal has to be to modify and maximize that, not overhaul it. In his best games, Williams has mixed some of the qualities that make Goff such a machine with his own knack for creating special plays out of thin air.</p><p>The reality for Williams and the Bears is that if there’s another team they can play poorly against and still beat, it’s the Saints. There would have to be a total meltdown to lose this one. But playing lackadaisically against them isn’t good for the long run as the team aspires to play in the Super Bowl.</p><p>Instead, this is a crucial game for Williams to reestablish the core of what he and Johnson have been working on.</p><p>This game can be the on-ramp to playing that way against much stronger opponents, such as the Lions next week or the Jaguars after that. The regular season ends with a rematch against the Vikings, who have allowed the fewest points and lowest passer rating in the NFL and shut down Williams before he got hurt in Week 2.</p><p>A monster game against the Saints would steady Williams just in time to navigate choppier waters ahead.</p>

entries.title: With towers redesigned, developer exhibits fresh plan for Goose Island site
entries.summary: <p>The developer Onni Group has sharpened details of its multiyear plan to bring high-density housing to Goose Island, a part of town long set aside for manufacturing.</p><p>Onni has shown fresh renderings to neighborhood groups and city officials highlighting open spaces, including an “urban beach” along the Chicago River, and varied architectural treatments for the planned towers.</p><p>Paul Purewal, Onni’s vice president of development, said the revisions emphasize amenities for incoming residents while showing that the project, called Halsted Pointe, can blend with communities to the north and west. Manufacturing is still prominent, but numerous residential and entertainment projects are taking root near Goose Island.</p><p>Onni already has started on the project’s first phase, a 46-story building at 931 N. Halsted St. Purewal said Onni is confident it can finance other phases even if interest rates continue to tick upward.</p><p>“The Chicago market is very strong compared to the demand in other markets,” he said. </p><p>Purewal said Onni is a long-term investor that can withstand inflation or economic slowdowns. The company projects it could complete Halsted Pointe in 2033, but extended timetables in development are often too optimistic.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Its original blueprint called for five buildings.</p><p>The site plan for the 8 acres includes pedestrian paths along the river and the North Branch Canal, dog runs, pickleball courts and a children’s playground. The property on the island’s southern end used to have a maintenance center for Greyhound buses.</p><p>Onni showed the revised plan Thursday to the Chicago Plan Commission, a courtesy appearance that required no vote.</p><p>Ald. Onni Group and SCB</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The estimated $1.4 billion investment marks the first incursion of housing onto Goose Island since city officials relaxed manufacturing-only zoning rules along the Chicago River’s North Branch in 2017. The industrial retention group North Branch Works negotiated with the city over that change. Its executive director, Jonathan Snyder, said he hopes Onni’s housing will help manufacturers attract a workforce that can rent apartments close by.</p><p>“We hope this will be a net positive to the extent that it creates a dense, walkable but still industrial-friendly development. That’s the challenge,” he said.</p><p>Onni also is behind <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/05/16/halsted-landing-onni-group-goose-island-renderings-mixed-use-development" >Halsted Landing</a>, a proposed $1.1 billion residential project wedged between Goose Island and the under-construction Bally’s casino.</p><p>However, it appears unlikely Halsted Landing will take off soon. The company has signed a 10-year agreement with Universal Destinations & Experiences to occupy part of the property, a former Tribune Co. building at 700 W. Chicago Ave.</p><p>The promised <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/river-west/2025/06/26/universal-horror-unleashed-theme-park-ballys-casino-comcast-world-business-chicago" >“immersive horror experience”</a> could be a placeholder that lets Onni earn money from the site before its bigger plan can jell.</p><p>Asked if Universal can be worked into the proposed residential enclave, Purewal said, “We’re weighing all the options.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/casinos-gambling/2026/11/17/ballys-560-million-loan-river-west-permanent-casino" >Bally’s announces $560 million loan to help bring construction of a permanent casino to the finish line</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
